_about: A world, as one file. Fill it in, then run:
and when it reports clean, run it again without --dry-run.
Every block has a `_help` key explaining what it is and what it may contain.
`_help` keys are stripped on import; leave them or delete them, it makes no
`_layer` on each block says who owns it (see LAYERS.md):
world  — yours, nothing else has an opinion
kit    — you are replacing an engine default; fine, and only affects you
`_status` says how far the engine consumes it today:
live     — read by the engine now
stored   — saved on the record, not yet read by anything
planned  — has no home yet; the importer will tell you and skip it

_help: Identity. Becomes the `worlds` row. `genre` seeds your calendar and tone
set, so pick it before those blocks. `theme` is a one-word steer used in
scene prompts (grounded, cozy, light-novel...).
`image_profile` must be one the appliance supports; leave it unless you
know you want another.
world.name: Gaia
world.tagline: Seven nations. Seven magics. One world worth living in.
world.description: A world of seven great nations, each born from a different culture and each touched by a different kind of magic. Dragons, yokai, djinn, and spirits are part of daily life. The peace is fraying, the Old Roads are broken, and somewhere a soul new to this world is about to choose where to begin.

_help: How the world sounds. The engine already enforces how narration BEHAVES
— second person, player agency, who can know what. This is the part that
is yours: register, refusals, and whether there is a named narrator.
`narrator` empty means a clean unnamed narrator, which is a real choice.
A named one is a character, and characters can be wrong — say what they
are not allowed to know.
`sample_paragraph` is the most useful field here. Four sentences of an
ordinary moment in the voice you want.
voice.register: Warm, close, unhurried. Concrete nouns, plain verbs. The narrator notices small things — the smell of tea, light through a paper screen, the sound of a wooden bridge under weight. It does not rush. It lets a moment sit before moving on. It is fond of this world without being sentimental.
never: No prophecy. No one is chosen. The world does not have a destiny for anyone.
No mid-scene worldbuilding exposition. Characters do not explain how magic works unless asked.
No scene closes on weather alone. Close on something alive — a person acting, a decision landing, a door left open.
No narrative omniscience about what a character feels. Describe what is visible, not what is private.
No grimdark narration. The world can be cruel, but the narration is not cruel.
No fourth-wall breaks. The narrator never addresses the player.
voice.sample_paragraph: The road to Haru's shrine climbs through cedar shade, the air cool and smelling of moss even in summer. A fox watches from the stones near the second torii gate, not moving, its eyes the color of dark tea. Below, the town spreads out in rooftops of grey tile and garden green, smoke rising from the bathhouse chimney in a thin, patient line. Someone is practicing the shamisen, and the notes drift up the hill like they have nowhere else to be.

_help: What every picture in this world carries. `global_prompt` is appended to
each image prompt; `negative_prompt` is ruled out of all of them.
The engine decides SIZE and FRAMING per record type and you cannot change
those — a scene renders 1216x832, a record 896x1152, a portrait 832x1216,
because those are the image model's native buckets. See LAYERS.md.
`entry_type_styles` overrides the engine's per-type defaults. Leave it
empty and you inherit sensible ones. Overriding a style does NOT remove
the framing tags — you can restyle your art, you cannot make it
uncroppable.
art._layer: world, except entry_type_styles which is kit
art.global_prompt: painterly anime illustration, warm natural light, soft atmospheric depth, detailed backgrounds with foliage and architecture, muted earth palette with warm gold accents, visible brush texture, gentle color gradients, studio-quality lighting, attention to daily-life details, food and interiors rendered with care, no text, no watermark, no border
art.negative_prompt: photorealistic, 3d render, dark grimdark palette, excessive gore, deformed hands, extra fingers, text overlays, watermark, signature, low detail background, flat shading

_help: Time. Leave this block out entirely and you get a calendar seeded from
your genre, which is usually enough to start.
`day_phases` is what the tracker shows instead of clock time.
`start` is where the campaign opens; `month_index` is zero-based.

festivals.name: Moon-Viewing Night
festivals.description: On the fullest night of Mistveil the shrines hang paper lanterns over their ponds and the whole capital gathers on rooftops to watch the moon's reflection — the one night the kami of the moon is said to walk among the shrines. Rival clans share sake on the tea-house balconies; even the Ashikara and Takeda send quiet emissaries to sit at the same low table. The shrine keepers read the moon's reflection for the year's fortune, and a clear reflection is taken as a good omen for the truce between the houses.

festivals.name: Blossom-Viewing
festivals.description: When the cherry trees of the capital bloom in Blossom month, the tea schools carry their kettles into the orchards and brew beneath the falling petals for any who pass. Samurai lay down their swords for the afternoon, the Yokai walk openly in the lantern-lit groves, and a blossom that lands in a cup of tea is kept and pressed as a charm for the year. It is the gentlest day in Tsukuyomi, and the one most often cited by foreigners as the reason they love the shogunate.

festivals.name: Dragonfire Vow
festivals.description: At Highsun the Dragon Order gathers on the high meadow beneath Sunhelm Keep and re-enacts the old binding-vows before the silent wyrms in the peaks above. Knights kneel in full armor and speak the fire-oaths to a ridge where nothing answers but wind — and yet the rite is never skipped, because the day the Order stops speaking is the day they admit the bond is truly dead. The common folk picnic on the lower slopes, the Dawnfire priests bless the knights, and the elves of Elfshade watch from the treeline, saying nothing.

festivals.name: Harvestmoon Mead-Feast
festivals.description: When the highland hives are opened in Amberfall, the mead-brewers of Rivenspire tap the first casks and the realm drinks the year's honey-wine together. The noble houses lay tables in Crossford's market square beside the merchant guild's stalls, and the baronesses and the river-traders toast each other with the same cup. It is the closest thing Valdris has to a day without rank, and the Greyfen thieves, it is said, take the night off — even a syndicate needs a feast.

festivals.name: Lantern Night
festivals.description: In Frost month the people of all three states set paper lanterns on the river and let them float toward the sea, each lantern carrying the name of someone lost in the Last War. Jin, Chu, and Wei each light their own bank of the river, and the three streams of light merge where the waters bend — the one night the truce is felt rather than merely obeyed. The strategists of the Jade Pavilion walk the banks unarmed, and for that night no one schemes against anyone.

festivals.name: The Three-States Tea Conclave
festivals.description: Each Greenreach the tea houses of Chudu host the one gathering where envoys of Jin, Chu, and Wei will sit in the same room — the Three-States Tea Conclave, where the year's trade disputes are settled over cups before they become border disputes. The Five Schools of Tea pour in turn, each state's envoy chooses a cup without knowing whose school brewed it, and the ancient etiquette is that no one may draw a blade until the last cup is drunk. It is diplomacy performed as ceremony, and it has held the truce more than once.

festivals.name: Jaguar Moon
festivals.description: On the brightest night of Harvest the deep-canopy tribes gather at the Alta Canopy's great bough-hall and the jaguar-kin run the Moon Hunt — a ceremonial pursuit through the canopy to honor the jaguar-spirit pact, taking a single marked deer and no more. The shamans of the Still Water Lodge chant the old pact-words by firelight, and the Council of the Seven Boughs meets in full session for the only time each year, hearing disputes beneath the moon until dawn. A hunt that takes more than the one deer is taken as a warning that the pact is fraying.

festivals.name: The Serpent-Waking
festivals.description: In Deepwinter the guardians of the Coiled Serpent temple climb to the pyramid summit and perform the Waking rite over the sealed spirit-gate — not to wake the serpent, but to assure it is still sleeping. A single flute is played down the gate-shaft and the note that returns is listened to by the eldest guardian: a clear echo means the seal holds, a wavering echo means the shamans must be summoned. The river-traders bring offerings of fruit and fish to the plaza below, and no outsider is permitted above the stair's first landing.

festivals.name: Midwinter Blot
festivals.description: At the darkest turn of Deepwinter every longhouse in Hrafnland lights the midwinter fire and the jarls perform the Blot — the old sacrifice to the frost-giants and the wights, offering the first of the preserved meat and the first mead so the long winter will not take more. The völur of the Fog-Mother coven cast the runes at the Bone-Circle and read the coming year aloud to the jarls, who are supposed to heed them and often do not. It is the one night no raids are sailed and no feud is pursued; even Erik Stone-eye's young raiders sit by the fire and listen.

festivals.name: Longship Launch
festivals.description: When Frostwane breaks and the fjord ice loosens, the Longkeel Brotherhood slides the first new longship of the year down the Drekahöfn slipway and the High Jarl blesses its prow with mead from the ancestral horn. The raid crews gather to claim their berths, the rune-carvers cut the warding-runes into the new keel while the crowd watches, and the Thing of the Frost-Jarls votes the summer raiding targets on the same shore. It is the day Hrafnland turns its face outward again, and the day the southern coasts begin watching the sea.

festivals.name: Saffron Harvest
festivals.description: At Highsun the saffron crocus blooms across the oasis-valleys and the Saffron Houses of Zaffar lead the harvest at dawn, when each purple flower must be picked before the desert sun wilts it. The whole city rises before light, the binding families and the spice merchants work the same fields for one day, and the Grand Bazaar closes so that everyone who can hold a basket is in the rows. The first saffron of the year is carried to the Saffron Palace on a great tray, and the Spice Queen declares the harvest open to trade — the day that sets Al-Khayzar's coin for the year.

festivals.name: The Night of True Names
festivals.description: In Snowend, when the desert nights are longest, the Circle of the Broken Road opens the Archive's star-chamber and the astrologers read the true-name charts beneath the winter constellations. The binding families send their heirs to learn the names they will one day need to command their djinn, and the scholars publicly debate a single point of the Pact's law until dawn — a tradition that is half scholarship and half theater. No djinn is called on this night; the binding families say it is out of respect, the scholars suspect it is because the stars make the calling too potent to risk.

festivals.name: The Great Pearl Dive
festivals.description: In Greenreach, when the reef waters run clearest, the Pearl-Blood Divers hold the Great Dive — the one day the deep reefs are opened to every atoll's divers together, and the season's first and finest pearls are brought up. The Council of Atolls watches from the canoes above, the tattoo-carvers mark each diver's chest with the day's dive-count, and the single largest pearl is offered back to the sea in a ceremony the wayfinders lead at dusk. It is the Archipelago's great day of wealth and pride, and the one day refugees are given equal right to the deep water.

festivals.name: The Rising Tide Memorial
festivals.description: At Thaw, when the year's highest water laps the atoll walls, the islanders walk the perimeter of each atoll at dusk and set floating lamps on the spot where a drowned island once stood. The names of the lost atolls are chanted by the wayfinders from the oldest canoes, the tattoo-carvers display the maps of places that no longer exist, and the refugees of the drowned islands lead the walk on the host atolls. It is the Archipelago's most solemn day — a reckoning with the rising sea that no feast follows, and the day the Council most often argues, afterward, about how many more they can shelter.

_help: What your campaign accumulates. Exactly SEVEN; five of one forges a
Momento — a real item linked to the scenes that earned it.
Leave this out to inherit seven seeded from your genre. If you write your
own, they should be moods a scene can be tagged with, not virtues. Avoid
borrowing another setting's cosmology; that is how a world ends up
wearing someone else's clothes.
`id` is lowercase and stable. `label` is what the panel shows.

set.label: Wonder
set.summary: The feeling of seeing a new place for the first time — a vista, a city, a creature, a sky that is different from the one you were born under.

set.label: Warmth
set.summary: A cozy moment — a shared meal, a bath, a conversation by firelight, the quiet pleasure of being somewhere safe.

set.label: Tension
set.summary: Something is about to break. The air before the argument, the silence before the attack, the pause before a decision that cannot be undone.

set.label: Peril
set.summary: Genuine danger. The ground is not safe. The body is at risk. Something here can hurt you.

set.label: Intrigue
set.summary: Politics, secrets, hidden motives. The sense that what is being said is not what is meant, and that the real conversation is happening somewhere else.

set.label: Sorrow
set.summary: Loss, longing, things that cannot be undone. The weight of what was and is no longer.

set.label: Resolve
set.summary: The moment before a decision. Not the decision itself — the breath before it, when the path is clear and the feet have not yet moved.

_help: Words this world uses for things the engine has generic names for. Keep
it short — this is pinned context and every line costs budget on every
turn. Only include words a narrator would get WRONG without being told.

terms.the currency: trade marks — small stamped metal discs accepted across all seven nations by weight
terms.the ruling body: varies by nation — shogun, king, warlord, jarl, council, or chief depending on where you are
terms.what people call outsiders: farfolk — used everywhere, mildly informal, not insulting
terms.what people call the reincarnated: god-touched — used in most nations; sometimes a compliment, sometimes a warning
terms.what people call the Old Roads: the Old Roads — no other name; everyone knows what you mean

_help: Places. `id` must be unique and is what everything else points at — use
`location:slug` and never change it afterwards.
`parent_location_id` builds the containment tree, and that tree is what
makes jurisdiction real: a patrol belonging to one polity has no business
inside another. Set it even for obvious things.
`map_size_ft` and `rooms` are only needed for interiors you will draw a
floorplan for. Leave them out for a region.

payload.summary: A quiet, luminous place above the clouds. Floating islands draped in mist, gardens that bloom in every season at once, and a pavilion at the center that looks down through layers of cloud to the world below. From the pavilion you can see all seven nations spread out like a map. The air is warm without being hot, still without being stale. It is mostly empty, and that emptiness is intentional — this is a place of choosing, not of living.
payload.jurisdiction: No one. The guide tends this place, but they do not rule it.
payload.terrain: Floating islands, gardens, mist, stone pavilion

payload.summary: A land of shrine-towns, hot-spring villages, terraced rice valleys, and castle-cities held by samurai clans. The supernatural is woven into daily life — fox spirits run message shops, tengu teach swordsmanship in mountain dojos, and the shrine network maintains the wards that keep wild yokai at a distance from settled areas. Cedar mountains, grey-tile rooftops, paper screens, the smell of incense and moss.
payload.jurisdiction: The Ashikara shogunate, nominally. The clans hold real power in their territories.
payload.terrain: Mountains, cedar forests, river valleys, coastlines

payload.summary: The capital of the Tsukuyomi Shogunate. A castle-city of grey tile and white plaster, built around the shogun's palace on its hill. The streets are clean, the shrines are well-kept, and the ward network hums with maintained power. Samurai walk the main streets; merchants crowd the river district; the tea houses near the south gate are where deals are made quietly. The old shogun has not been seen in public this season.
payload.jurisdiction: Direct rule of the Ashikara shogunate. The city magistrate handles daily governance.
payload.terrain: Hilltop palace, river district, lowland merchant quarters

payload.summary: A mountain hot-spring village built along a single road that climbs from the valley to an old shrine at the top. Cedar shade, moss on the stone steps, steam rising from the bathhouse. A fox watches from the torii gate. The shrine keeper, Miko Sora, maintains the ward for this stretch of the Cedar Road. Shamisen music drifts down from somewhere above. The town has a tea house, a general store, a stable, and about two hundred people who mostly know each other.
payload.jurisdiction: Ashikara territory, but the nearest magistrate is a day's ride away. The shrine keeper is the closest thing to authority here.
payload.terrain: Mountain slope, cedar forest, hot springs

payload.summary: A kingdom of stone castles, green hills, deep forests, and mountain passes where dragons roost. Humans, elves, dwarves, and halflings live here in an uneasy alliance held together by old oaths. The dragon-bonded knights — once the kingdom's strongest defenders — have not received a new bond in a generation. The kingdom is old and it knows it. Stone and banners, the sound of hooves on a bridge, wind in the high towers.
payload.jurisdiction: The Crown of Valdris, seated in Crownhaven. Noble houses hold territories under the crown's authority.
payload.terrain: Rolling hills, deep forests, mountains, rivers

payload.summary: The capital of Valdris. A city of white stone and seven towers, built on a hill above the Greywine River. The king's castle dominates the skyline, its banners worn by weather. The knightly order's chapter house stands near the castle gate, quieter than it used to be. The market square is still busy — Valdris is prosperous — but the conversations in the taverns turn to succession and the dragons' silence. About a hundred thousand people live here.
payload.jurisdiction: Direct rule of the Crown. The city watch handles daily order.
payload.terrain: Hilltop city, river port, surrounding farmland

payload.summary: The mountain fortress of the dragon-bonded knightly order, built into the peaks above Crownhaven. Stone walls scarred by dragonfire, a courtyard wide enough for a dragon to land, and a hall where the bonded knights once gathered. The hall is half-empty now. The old knights maintain the traditions; the younger ones question them. The dragons roost higher in the mountains and do not come down.
payload.jurisdiction: Self-governed by the knightly order under a charter from the Crown. The Crown has not tested that independence in decades.
payload.terrain: Mountain peak, stone fortress, dragon roosts above

payload.summary: A vast land of river valleys, terraced mountains, silk-road trade, and walled cities, held in an uneasy truce between three states: Jin in the north, Chu in the south, and Wei in the west. Politics is the primary battlefield. Martial arts and chi cultivation are practiced by soldiers and monks. Scholar-strategists advise warlords. Silk and lacquer, the sound of a guqin at night, ink on rice paper.
payload.jurisdiction: Divided between three states: Jin, Chu, and Wei. Each is ruled by a warlord and their court.
payload.terrain: River valleys, terraced mountains, plains, highland plateaus

payload.summary: The northern capital of Jin, and the largest city in Gaia. Two hundred thousand people live within its walls. Wide boulevards, canal crossings, the warlord's palace on the central hill, and the Great Academy where scholars learn strategy and philosophy. The markets are enormous — silks from Chu, iron from Wei, spices from Al-Khayzar via the Old Road. The truce is three years old, and the younger officers at the Academy speak openly about how it should end.
payload.jurisdiction: Direct rule of the Jin warlord. City magistrates handle daily governance; the warlord's court handles everything else.
payload.terrain: Walled city, canals, hilltop palace, surrounding farmland

payload.summary: A vast rainforest threaded by rivers, where stone cities are built into the canopy and the jungle is alive. No single government — a network of tribes and city-states connected by river trade and shared spiritual tradition. Temple cities of an old civilization stand deep in the jungle, half-reclaimed, still humming with power. Green light through leaves, the sound of water and birds, painted skin and featherwork.
payload.jurisdiction: No central authority. Each tribe and city-state is self-governing. Disputes are settled by river-court or shamanic mediation.
payload.terrain: Rainforest, rivers, waterfalls, temple ruins

payload.summary: The river capital of Verdania, built on stilts over a great river. Houses of woven wood and painted clay, connected by walkways and canoe bridges. The market floats — boats and rafts selling fish, fruit, feathers, and herbs. The river-folk are the majority here. The shamans' hall sits at the center of the city, the largest structure, where the elder shamans maintain the oldest spirit-pacts. The river is rising, and the lowest walkways are already underwater at high tide.
payload.jurisdiction: Governed by a council of tribal elders and the shamans' hall. Decisions are made by consensus, slowly.
payload.terrain: River city on stilts, floating market, surrounding jungle

payload.summary: A land of fjords, longships, sea-sagas, and the long dark of winter. No king — each fjord is ruled by a jarl, and the jarls meet once a year at the Althing to settle disputes and make laws. Traders, raiders, and storytellers who believe a life worth living is one worth singing about. Frost giants live in the deep mountains and are best left alone. Cold, salt, wood-smoke, the creak of a longship, aurora over black water.
payload.jurisdiction: Each fjord is ruled by a jarl. The Althing settles disputes between jarls once a year.
payload.terrain: Fjords, mountains, sea, tundra

payload.summary: The largest trading port in Hrafnland. A fjord town of longhouses and warehouses, shipyards and mead halls, built where the fjord meets the open sea. Longships line the dock. Traders from Valdris and the Tide Archipelago exchange goods here — iron for spice, furs for silk. Jarl Sigrid Hallvarsdottir holds this fjord, and her mead hall is the loudest place in town on a winter night. The aurora is bright this year, and the volur say that means something.
payload.jurisdiction: Ruled by Jarl Sigrid Hallvarsdottir. The jarl's household guards keep order; the Althing handles disputes between fjords.
payload.terrain: Fjord port, longhouses, shipyards, surrounding cliffs

payload.summary: A land of desert city-states, spice markets, oasis gardens, and starlit caravanserais. Djinn walk the markets in human form. A confederation of city-states bound by trade and the Pact of the Lamp — an agreement that no city will war upon another, enforced by djinn older than any dynasty. Golden, warm, perfumed. The sound of water in a fountain, spice and cardamom, stars over sand.
payload.jurisdiction: A confederation of city-states, each self-governed, bound by the Pact of the Lamp. The djinn enforce the pact.
payload.terrain: Desert, oases, mountain passes, coastal trade ports

payload.summary: The spice capital of Al-Khayzar. A city of domes and minarets, sun-baked sandstone walls, and narrow streets that open suddenly into courtyard markets. The Star Bazaar opens after sundown and runs until dawn — lanterns, silk canopies, the smell of cardamom and saffron. The old binding families have their estates in the high city, where the contracts with djinn are kept in vaults. The Pact of the Lamp holds here, and the djinn who enforce it are visible in the market — a figure of blue fire haggling over the price of dates is not unusual.
payload.jurisdiction: Governed by the Council of Binding Families, under the Pact of the Lamp. The djinn enforce the pact when called upon.
payload.terrain: Desert city, walled quarters, oasis, surrounding dunes

payload.summary: A warm-water world of hundreds of islands, big and small, connected by wayfinding and song. The voyagers are the greatest navigators in Gaia, reading stars, currents, and birds across open water. No central authority — each island has its own chief or council, and the wayfinder guilds serve as messengers, diplomats, and historians. The sea levels are rising, and the voyagers are being pushed inward. Warm, salt, open. The sound of waves on a reef, stars and warm wind, tattoo patterns and carved wood.
payload.jurisdiction: Each island is self-governed by a chief or council. The wayfinder guilds mediate between islands.
payload.terrain: Islands, reefs, open ocean, volcanic peaks

payload.summary: The central gathering island of the Tide Archipelago. A ring of low islands around a calm lagoon, connected by canoe bridges and walkways. The great meeting house sits on the largest island, open-walled, facing the sea. This is where the wayfinder guilds meet and where inter-island disputes are settled. The shore has crept inward — the outer islets that used to hold fishing huts are underwater now. The lagoon is still beautiful, turquoise and calm, but the people here talk about where they will go when the water comes for the meeting house.
payload.jurisdiction: Governed by a council of island chiefs, with the wayfinder guilds as advisors and mediators.
payload.terrain: Coral atoll, lagoon, low islands, canoe bridges

payload.summary: The great port city of the Tsukuyomi Shogunate, where the Kawa River spills into the Moonshade Sea. A sprawl of wooden piers, tile-roofed warehouses, and salt-weathered merchant houses pressed against a curving harbor. The smell of tar, fish, and wet rope hangs over everything, cut by charcoal smoke from the street stalls. Junks and coastal traders crowd the moorings; yokai-touched fog rolls in on certain mornings and the harbor wardstones glow faint blue to keep the mist from reaching the granaries. The city is loud — gulls, dock shouts, the bell of the harbor shrine marking the turn of every watch. The Ashikara-appointed harbor master collects duties here, but the merchant guilds hold the real leverage, and everyone knows it. About thirty thousand people live and work in Kawazaki, plus a floating population of sailors, pilgrims, and yokai who do not always trouble to be counted.
payload.jurisdiction: Ashikara territory, governed by an appointed harbor master and a council of the five largest merchant guilds. The guilds set trade policy; the harbor master collects the shogunate's cut.
payload.terrain: Coastal harbor, river delta, tidal flats, surrounding fishing villages

payload.summary: The beating heart of Kawazaki — a crescent of piers and moorings wide enough to hold two hundred vessels. Long pontoons of dark cedar bob in the swell, lashed together with rope the color of rust. Stevedores haul rice sacks and lacquer crates; a kappa works the rope coils on the eastern pier, tolerated because no one ties a knot faster. The harbor shrine sits at the end of the main pier, a small red torii above the tide line, where sailors drop copper coins before a voyage. The harbor master's tower rises at the harbor's throat, flying the Ashikara mon. Fog horns sound at dusk. The water is dark and cold and moves with things that are not always fish.
payload.jurisdiction: Direct control of the harbor master's office under the Ashikara shogunate. Dockside disputes are settled at the master's tower; serious crimes go to the city magistrate.
payload.terrain: Open harbor, cedar piers, tidal water, stone seawall

payload.summary: A vast open hall of timber and tile just inland of the harbor, where the morning's catch is auctioned before the fog burns off. Sawdust on the floor, blood on the gutting tables, the cold mineral smell of the sea and the sharp bite of fresh-cut ginger. Fishmongers shout prices in a clipped code no outsider can follow. The catch is ordinary at first glance — mackerel, sea bream, squid — but a knowing buyer can find river-spirit carp, glow-bellied lanternfish pulled from the deep channels, and once a season something pulled from the water that the auctioneer will not name aloud. The kappa dockworkers are banned from the auction floor after an incident two years ago that no one will describe in detail.
payload.jurisdiction: Run by the Fishmongers' Guild under a charter from the harbor master. Guild wardens police the floor; the guild sets the auction schedule and the tariff on exotic catch.
payload.terrain: Covered market hall, stone gutting floors, ice cellars below

payload.summary: The oldest shrine in Kawazaki, set on a rise above the warehouse district where the harbor wardstones are anchored. A modest building — unpainted cedar, a mossy torii, paper lanterns replaced more often than the shrine keeper would like. The real structure is below ground: a chamber where the ward network's anchor stones pulse with slow blue light, maintained by a lineage of shrine keepers who have served since before the Ashikara came to power. The keeper, an old woman named Ume-no-ji, can read the wards the way a physician reads a pulse. When the fog brings something hungry, the shrine is the first to know. Pilgrims come here to ask safe passage; sailors come to leave offerings. Both are listened to, in different ways.
payload.jurisdiction: An independent shrine lineage, nominally under the Ashikara shrine network but older than it. The shrine keeper's authority over the wards is not contested; her authority over anything else is politely ignored.
payload.terrain: Hillside shrine, subterranean ward chamber, moss garden

payload.summary: The narrow lanes behind the harbor where the tea houses, sake dens, and river-girl establishments press shoulder to shoulder. Lantern light on wet stone, the sound of shamisen and a low drum, the smell of plum wine and pipe smoke and something sweeter from the upper rooms. This is where merchant deals are closed that the harbor master will never hear about, where samurai come off the ships and spend a season's pay in a night, and where a yokai in a painted face will pour your drink and ask you questions you will answer before you realize you have. The quarter is run by the Tea House Guild, and the guild is run by a woman no one has ever seen clearly. It is the loudest, warmest, most dangerous part of Kawazaki.
payload.jurisdiction: The Tea House Guild governs the quarter under a private arrangement with the merchant guilds. The harbor master's men do not enter without an invitation. The guild keeps its own peace — harshly.
payload.terrain: Narrow lanes, multi-story tea houses, lantern-lit courtyards

payload.summary: A castle town in the western foothills held by the Kagami clan, the Ashikara's oldest rival. The castle itself sits on a steep ridge above the river — black-timbered, iron-roofed, built to be held against a shogun. The town below has grown rich and sullen in its shadow. Forges ring day and night; the Kagami have been the finest swordsmiths in Tsukuyomi for five generations, and their steel is the one thing the Ashikara cannot match. The streets are wider than the capital's and better drained, the houses sturdier, the samurai district nearly as large as the merchant quarter. There is a calm here that is the calm of a place that knows its own strength and is waiting. Daimyo Kagami Renji has not attended the shogun's court in three years. His replies to summons are courteous, and empty.
payload.jurisdiction: Held by the Kagami clan under a grant older than the Ashikara shogunate. The daimyo governs directly; the shogun's writ runs here only with the Kagami's consent, which is rarely given.
payload.terrain: Ridge castle, river valley, forge district, terraced hillsides

payload.summary: The black castle on the ridge. Iron roof tiles that turn the rain the color of old blood, timber walls braced with bands of Kagami steel, and a central keep six stories high that can see the river road for miles in every direction. The inner bailey houses the Kagami household and two hundred retainers; the outer bailey holds the armory, the stables, and the guest hall where visiting samurai are received — and counted. The castle has never fallen. The walls are warded, though the Kagami wards are older and stranger than the Ashikara network, cut with symbols the shrine network does not use. Daimyo Kagami Renji holds court in the upper keep. He is fifty, calm, and rumored to be the best swordsman in the west. No one has tested the rumor.
payload.jurisdiction: Seat of the Kagami clan. The daimyo's word is absolute within the castle grounds. No outside authority — shogunate, shrine, or magistrate — has jurisdiction inside the walls.
payload.terrain: Ridge-top fortress, stone foundations, iron-roofed keeps, warded walls

payload.summary: The district below the castle where the smiths work, built along the river for the water wheels that drive the bellows. The air tastes of charcoal and hot iron; the sound of hammers is constant, a rhythm the town sleeps to. The master smiths are Kagami vassals by blood, and their forging secrets are passed father to son with an oath that is said to bind even after death. The finest blades in Tsukuyomi come out of these forges — folded steel with a hamon like frozen moonlight on water. A blade from the Forge Quarter is a status symbol in the capital, and a practical one on the battlefield. The smiths will not sell to the Ashikara directly. The blades reach the capital through intermediaries, at a markup, and the Kagami pretend not to notice.
payload.jurisdiction: Kagami clan territory. The master smiths answer to the daimyo. The forge quarter has its own internal guild structure, but the guild head is appointed by the clan.
payload.terrain: Riverfront workshops, water wheels, charcoal stores, tempering pools

payload.summary: The orderly grid of walled compounds where the Kagami retainers live, on the slope between the castle and the forge quarter. Each compound is built around a small training yard; the sound of wooden swords on wood carries across the district from dawn. The retainers are loyal — not bought, not bullied, but bound by generations of service and the simple fact that the Kagami have never lost. The district has its own bathhouse, its own small shrine to the clan's founder, and a dojo where the senior retainers teach a sword style the Kagami do not allow to be taught anywhere else. The retainers' children play in the lanes with wooden swords before they can read. It is quiet here, and watchful.
payload.jurisdiction: Direct administration of the Kagami clan. A senior retainer serves as district head; internal discipline is handled by the clan, not the magistrate.
payload.terrain: Walled compounds, training yards, steep lanes, clan shrine

payload.summary: The open market that runs along the riverbank below the forge quarter, where the town's commercial life happens in full view of the castle. Stalls of river fish, hill rice, mountain vegetables, charcoal, and the imported goods that reach Kaeden over the western passes — wool, leather, a little southern silk. The market is less frenetic than a port city's, but the money that moves here is old money, and the merchants know their place. A tengu runs a stall selling mountain herbs and advice, and is tolerated because the herbs are genuine and the advice is occasionally useful. The market square has a stone where public notices are posted, and a small magistrate's office that handles debts and minor disputes. Serious matters go up the hill.
payload.jurisdiction: Town magistrate under Kagami appointment handles trade disputes and debt. The clan takes a tithe of market goods; the magistrate collects it.
payload.terrain: Riverbank market square, stone notice post, magistrate's office

payload.summary: A mountain monastery town built into the terraced slopes of the White Crane range, where the great training monastery of the Shirogane order has stood for three hundred years. The town climbs the mountain in steps — pilgrim lodgings at the base, tea houses and supply shops in the middle, and the monastery itself at the top, a sprawling complex of dark wood halls and gold-leafed temples connected by covered stairways and stone paths worn smooth by a century of feet. Tengu roost in the upper pines and teach swordsmanship to those they judge worthy; the monks maintain a library of scrolls older than any clan. The air is thin, cold, and smells of cedar and incense and the ozone of old ward-work. Pilgrims come up the mountain road in a steady stream. Some come back changed. Some do not come back. The town is small — perhaps three thousand permanent residents — but the monastery's influence reaches across Tsukuyomi.
payload.jurisdiction: The Shirogane order governs the town and the monastery. The order is technically independent of both shogunate and clan; in practice, it maintains careful neutrality and is left alone by all sides because no one wants the tengu as an enemy.
payload.terrain: Terraced mountainside, cedar forest, monastery complex, pilgrim road

payload.summary: The great monastery at the summit — six halls of dark timber and sweeping eaves, a gold-leafed main temple, a library built into the rock of the peak itself, and a training ground of packed earth where monks and tengu practice together at dawn. The abbot, an ancient monk named Tesshin, is said to have studied under a tengu master and to be older than the current shogun's grandfather. The library holds scrolls on ward-craft, yokai lore, and martial philosophy that exist nowhere else; access is granted by the abbot alone, and he grants it rarely. The main temple's altar holds a shard of wardstone that hums with a frequency that makes the teeth ache. The air here is very still. Time moves differently at the top of the mountain, and the monks will tell you so without smiling.
payload.jurisdiction: Self-governed by the Shirogane order under the abbot. The order recognizes no external civil authority over the monastery grounds. This independence has been respected, warily, for three centuries.
payload.terrain: Summit temple complex, rock-cut library, training grounds, wardstone altar

payload.summary: A clearing in the upper pines above the monastery, where the tengu who roost in the White Crane range come to teach — or to test. The ground is packed earth and old needles, ringed by cedar so tall the sky is a narrow strip above. Wooden posts stand in a circle, scarred by centuries of sword cuts. The tengu teach a sword style that has no name and no written form; it is learned in the body or not at all. They accept students by judgment alone — some are turned away at the treeline, some are tested for a season and released, and a very few are taught. A tengu lesson leaves bruises that heal slowly and insights that do not heal at all. The monks do not come here. The tengu do not come to the monastery. The arrangement is old and understood.
payload.jurisdiction: The tengu govern their own grounds by their own customs. The monastery acknowledges their sovereignty over the clearing and the upper forest. No civil authority reaches here.
payload.terrain: Forest clearing, packed earth, scarred training posts, upper cedar canopy

payload.summary: The lower town, where the pilgrim road meets the first terraces and the town begins. Lodging houses, tea stalls, incense shops, and sellers of prayer beads and ward-talismans line the steep main street. The air is warmer here than above — woodsmoke, cooking rice, the sweet rot of fallen cedar needles. Pilgrims rest here before the final climb; many leave offerings at the small wayside shrine at the quarter's top, where a fox spirit is said to judge the sincerity of the prayer. The townspeople are patient with the endless flow of visitors; their living depends on it. A bathhouse at the quarter's center is fed by a hot spring, and it is the last warm water a pilgrim will see before the monastery.
payload.jurisdiction: Town administration under the Shirogane order. A lay steward appointed by the abbot handles lodging regulations, market disputes, and the pilgrim tax that funds the town's upkeep.
payload.terrain: Terraced streets, pilgrim lodgings, hot spring bathhouse, wayside shrine

payload.summary: The rock-cut archive beneath the main temple, where the order's scrolls are kept in dry, warded chambers that smell of old paper and cedar oil and something faintly electric. Racks of bamboo and lacquered wood hold thousands of scrolls — ward-craft treatises, yokai catalogs, clan histories older than the Ashikara, martial manuals, and a sealed section the abbot will not discuss. A single monk, the Keeper of Records, holds the keys. Copies of certain scrolls are made available to scholars and shrine keepers who petition the abbot and are approved; the originals never leave the chambers. The air is still and cool and the ward-hum is strong enough that visitors sometimes hear it in their teeth. A fire here would be a catastrophe measured in centuries, and the order has built accordingly — stone walls, warded doors, and a single narrow entrance.
payload.jurisdiction: Under the direct authority of the abbot and the Keeper of Records. Access is by abbot's grant only. No civil or clan authority may enter or demand scrolls.
payload.terrain: Underground chambers, stone racks, warded doors, single entrance

payload.summary: A fortress town at the northern edge of Tsukuyomi, where the Cedar Road meets the Frostspine passes and the wild yokai come down out of the deep mountains when the snows drive them. The town is built for defense — a stockade of iron-banded cedar, a central keep on a granite knob, narrow streets that funnel an attacker into killing grounds. The garrison flies the Ashikara mon but the soldiers are a hard mix of clan retainers, ronin, and mountain folk who have fought the yokai all their lives. The cold is the real ruler here. Frost rims the eaves eight months of the year, and the ward fires burn blue at the gates. The town smells of pine resin, smoke, and the iron tang of the forge that never stops, because a broken wardstone in Kitagoe is not an inconvenience — it is a death sentence for someone. Two thousand people live here, and most of them can use a weapon. They do not grow rice. They grow survivors.
payload.jurisdiction: Ashikara territory under a military governor appointed by the shogunate. The governor commands the garrison; in practice, the veteran sergeants and the mountain-folk scouts have more say in daily survival than any appointed official.
payload.terrain: Mountain pass fortress, granite keep, stockade walls, surrounding pine forest

payload.summary: The granite knob at the town's center, crowned by a squat three-story keep of dark stone and iron-banded timber. The walls are thick enough that the winter wind does not reach the inner halls. The governor's quarters are on the top floor; the garrison command room is on the second, where a map of the northern passes covers an entire wall, marked with pins for yokai sightings, patrol routes, and the names of posts where soldiers have died. The ground floor is an armory and a wardstone-charging chamber, where the gate wardstones are renewed on a rotation that no one dares miss. The keep has a well cut into the granite that has never run dry. The roof mounts a signal fire that, lit, can be seen by the next post down the Cedar Road within the hour.
payload.jurisdiction: Seat of the military governor. The keep is under direct shogunate military authority; the governor's word is law within its walls.
payload.terrain: Granite knob, stone-and-timber keep, armory, wardstone chamber, signal fire

payload.summary: The shrine at the north gate, small and smoky and far more important than its size suggests. A single priest, an old man named Jiro who lost his left hand to a frost-oni twenty years ago, tends the gate wardstones and the shrine's blue fires that burn at the stockade threshold in all weather. The wardstones here are heavier, cruder, and more frequently replaced than those of the lowland cities — the northern yokai hit harder, and the stones crack under the strain. Jiro keeps a rack of spares and recharges them on a forge he built into the shrine's back wall. Offerings are left by soldiers going on patrol: sake, salt, a lock of hair. Some come back to collect the hair. Many do not. The shrine is the thin line between the town and what lives in the deep mountains, and everyone in Kitagoe knows it.
payload.jurisdiction: Under the Ashikara shrine network, but effectively autonomous due to distance. The priest answers to the network in principle and to the garrison governor in practice; neither checks on him often.
payload.terrain: Gate-side shrine, wardstone forge, blue fire basins, spare wardstone rack

payload.summary: A long, low building of pine logs near the north gate, home to the mountain-folk scouts who are the garrison's eyes in the deep forest. The hall smells of pine resin, damp wool, and the musk of something the scouts will not name. The scouts are not clan retainers; they are hunters, trappers, and hermits who know the Frostspine the way a fisherman knows the sea. They track yokai movements, mark safe paths through the snow, and occasionally bring back things — pelts, bones, a wardstone shard found in a place no wardstone should be. The hall's walls are hung with maps drawn on birch bark, updated after every patrol. The scout chief, a weathered woman named Beni, has a working arrangement with a tengu who nests in the upper peaks; the details are private, and no one has survived asking twice.
payload.jurisdiction: The scouts operate semi-independently under the garrison governor's commission. Beni manages her own people, her own routes, and her own arrangements; the governor signs the commissions and does not ask questions.
payload.terrain: Pine-log hall, birch-bark map walls, equipment stores, staging yard

payload.summary: The town forge, which never goes cold. A stone building near the keep with two hearths, a charcoal bin that is refilled daily, and a smith named Goro who is the third generation of his family to hold the position. The forge turns out wardstone casings, gate hardware, arrowheads, and the heavy shortswords the garrison prefers for close work against things that do not stop when a human would. Goro also repairs wardstone brackets — the iron bands that hold the stones in place at the gates and along the stockade — and he has a reputation for being able to reseat a cracked stone well enough to hold for one more winter. The forge is loud, hot, and the one place in Kitagoe that feels like it is winning. Sparks fly into the snow and die hissing.
payload.jurisdiction: Town administration under the military governor. The smith is a civilian appointee, but the position is effectively hereditary; the governor signs the commission and Goro does the work.
payload.terrain: Stone forge, twin hearths, charcoal stores, snow yard

payload.summary: The shogun's palace on its hill, visible from every quarter of the capital — white plaster walls, dark grey tile, and a five-story main keep that catches the moonlight that gives the city its name. The outer wards are administrative halls where the city magistrate and the shogunate's clerks conduct the business of governance. The inner wards are the Ashikara household's private quarters, closed to all but family and the most senior retainers. The old shogun has not been seen in the inner gardens this season, and the senior retainers take his instructions through a screen. The palace wardstones are the strongest in the nation, maintained by the shrine network's master keeper, and they hum at a frequency that makes yokai uneasy within the walls. The throne room is kept ready. The moon-throne has not been sat in publicly since autumn.
payload.jurisdiction: Seat of the Ashikara shogunate. The palace is under the shogun's direct authority; the city magistrate handles the city below but has no jurisdiction within the palace grounds.
payload.terrain: Hilltop palace, administrative outer wards, private inner wards, warded gardens

payload.summary: The commercial heart of the capital, built along the Moon River where it curves through the low town. Warehouses, counting houses, and merchant mansions of dark timber and white plaster line the embankment, their eaves nearly touching across the narrower lanes. The smell of river water, incense from the district shrine, and the green tea served in every counting house. This is where the nation's wealth is counted and moved — rice tithes, silk, silver from the western mines, all flowing through the river district's books. The merchant guilds are powerful here, and their relationship with the shogunate's magistrates is a careful balance of favors and tariffs. The river bridges are hung with lanterns at night, and the district is beautiful in a way that makes it easy to forget that fortunes are destroyed here as calmly as they are made.
payload.jurisdiction: City magistrate under the Ashikara shogunate. The merchant guilds hold significant informal power; the magistrate governs with their cooperation or not at all.
payload.terrain: River embankment, merchant mansions, warehouses, lantern bridges

payload.summary: The head shrine of the Ashikara ward network, set on a rise between the palace and the river district. A complex of cedar halls and moss gardens centered on a main sanctuary where the network's master keeper conducts the rituals that bind the nation's wardstones to their anchors. The shrine is the largest in Tsukuyomi — six priests, twelve acolytes, and a library of ward-craft that is smaller than the Shirogane archive but more current. The master keeper, a stern woman named Karin, is one of the few people the old shogun still sees regularly, and no one knows what is said in those meetings. The shrine's central wardstone is the network's root anchor; if it fails, every wardstone in the nation feels it. It has not failed. The shrine keeps a fox spirit in the inner garden, bound by an old pact, who carries messages between the network's shrines faster than any horse.
payload.jurisdiction: The Ashikara shrine network, under the master keeper. The shrine is technically independent of the shogunate's civil authority, but the master keeper's relationship with the shogun blurs that line.
payload.terrain: Cedar shrine complex, moss gardens, central wardstone sanctuary, fox-bound garden

payload.summary: The tea house district near the south gate, where the deals that the magistrate's office will never hear about are made over cups of matcha and something stronger. The quarter is a maze of lanes, each tea house narrower than the last, lanterns hung so low a tall man must duck. The establishment at the quarter's heart — the Moonfaced House — is where the senior retainers meet the merchant guild heads, where clan envoys deliver messages too delicate for paper, and where a person can learn what the shogun's health really is, if they know whom to ask and can afford the price. The quarter is quiet by design; the tea house guild keeps the peace with a firmness that rivals the magistrate's. The shamisen plays late. The lanterns burn low. The conversations do not repeat.
payload.jurisdiction: City magistrate's territory, but the tea house guild maintains its own order. The magistrate's men patrol the main lanes; the guild handles the rest, and the two arrangements do not overlap.
payload.terrain: Narrow lanes, multi-story tea houses, lantern-hung eaves, discreet gardens

payload.summary: The ordered grid of walled compounds on the slope between the palace and the river district, where the Ashikara retainers and the houses of the loyal clans maintain their city residences. The lanes are swept, the walls are whitewashed, and the gates carry the mon of the houses within. The district is quieter than the river district and colder than the tea quarter — this is where the shogunate's military and administrative class lives, and the atmosphere is one of controlled formality. Each compound has a training yard; the sound of practice is the district's dawn bell. The senior retainers' houses are nearest the palace, their compounds larger, their walls higher. The younger retainers and the lesser clan houses are further down the slope, where the lanes narrow and the formality eases, very slightly, into something almost like a neighborhood.
payload.jurisdiction: Direct administration of the Ashikara shogunate. A senior retainer serves as district head; the city magistrate does not enter the samurai district without the district head's consent.
payload.terrain: Walled compounds, training yards, swept lanes, hillside slope

payload.summary: The hot spring bathhouse at the village's center, fed by the spring that gives Haru's Shrine Town its reason to exist. A low building of cedar and stone, steam rising through the slats of the changing room, the mineral smell of the water sharp and clean. The bath is a single pool, natural rock lined with smooth stone, hot enough to turn the skin red in minutes. The villagers gather here at dusk — the shrine keeper, the store owner, the stable master, the farmers — and the talk that happens in the steam is the village's real government. A partitioned section is reserved for the fox spirits who maintain the message shop; they bathe separately and later, and their water is said to be warmer. Travelers are welcomed for a small fee and a respectful quiet. The water is said to ease old wounds, and it does.
payload.jurisdiction: Village commons, maintained collectively. The shrine keeper oversees the spring's ward and settles any dispute over usage; no outside authority has ever needed to intervene.
payload.terrain: Cedar bathhouse, natural hot spring pool, stone lining, steam changing room

payload.summary: The old shrine at the top of the village's single road, where the torii stands mossy and the cedar shade is thickest. A small sanctuary — one hall, one altar, one wardstone that anchors this stretch of the Cedar Road's protection. The shrine keeper, Miko Sora, lives in the attached cottage and has maintained the ward for longer than the village's memory of anyone else doing so. The wardstone is modest compared to the capital's, but it is well-tended, and the fox that watches from the torii at dusk is, by village reputation, the same fox that has watched for decades. Pilgrims and travelers leave offerings here before continuing up or down the Cedar Road. The shrine smells of cedar, moss, and the faint ozone of a wardstone under steady care. Shamisen music drifts down from somewhere above, and no one is entirely sure who plays it.
payload.jurisdiction: The Ashikara shrine network, represented by the shrine keeper. In practice, the shrine keeper is the village's authority; the network's oversight is remote and infrequent.
payload.terrain: Hilltop shrine, mossy torii, cedar shade, wardstone altar, keeper's cottage

payload.summary: The single general store, halfway up the village road, where anything a traveler or a villager needs can be found if the owner, Tama, has it or can get it. The store is a front room of packed-earth floor and cedar shelves holding rice, dried fish, lamp oil, rope, sandals, prayer cord, mountain herbs, and a few luxuries that arrive on the peddler's back once a month — sake, salt, a bolt of cloth. Tama knows everyone in the village and most of what they need. The store is also the village's post point; messages bound for the Cedar Road's next shrine are left here for the fox-spirit courier. A board by the door carries notices — weather warnings, road conditions, the occasional missing person. The store smells of dried fish and cedar and the faint sweetness of the sake jars in the back.
payload.jurisdiction: Private business under village custom. Tama answers to the shrine keeper for the courier arrangement and to herself for everything else.
payload.terrain: Roadside store, packed-earth floor, cedar shelves, notice board

payload.summary: A small establishment near the shrine, run by a fox spirit who goes by the name Kiko and maintains the message service that links Haru's Shrine Town to the next ward-point along the Cedar Road. The shop is a single room with a low desk, a charcoal brazier, and a cushion that is always warm, as if someone had just left it. Messages are written on thin paper, folded into fox-tags, and delivered along the ward-line by courier foxes faster than any horse — though only to shrines on the network, and only for those the foxes choose to serve. Kiko charges in copper or in favors, and her ledger of favors is longer than her ledger of coin. She is polite, sharp, and old in a way that does not show. The villagers treat her with careful respect. The shrine keeper treats her as a colleague.
payload.jurisdiction: The fox spirit's own authority, under a pact with the Ashikara shrine network. Kiko operates independently; the shrine keeper coordinates with her but does not direct her.
payload.terrain: Single-room shop, low desk, charcoal brazier, courier fox runs

payload.summary: Deep within the ancient Thornwhisper Forest, where the canopy grows so thick that noontime feels like dusk, the elven city of Elfshade rises not on stone foundations but upon living wood and woven light. Bridges of pale birch bark arch between colossal oaks, and homes spiral around trunks in graceful helices of carved wood and stained glass that catch what little sun filters through. Lanterns of captured starlight—enchanted by the Valdris Elves who have inhabited these woods for six thousand years—glow a soft silver-blue at all hours, casting the mossy pathways in an eternal twilight. The air smells of pine resin, wet bark, and the faint sweetness of night-blooming jasmine that climbs every railing. Song spills from open windows, and silver-haired elves in flowing robes move between terraces with unhurried grace, their footsteps silent on the living wood. Though Elfshade swore fealty to the crown of Valdris three centuries ago, its people keep their own counsel, and a traveler who enters without an elven guide is said to walk in circles for hours before finding the city's heart.
payload.jurisdiction: Ruled by the Thornwhisper Court, a council of elven elders presided over by Lord-Councilor Ithilandel. The city nominally answers to the Crown of Valdris but is granted broad autonomy in internal matters by the Treaty of Silver Leaves. Royal tax collectors are permitted entry only on the equinoxes.
payload.terrain: Ancient temperate forest with dense canopy, mossy floor, and natural streams

payload.summary: Straddling the great Greyfen River at the place where it narrows to a thundering gorge before spilling toward the southern sea, Rivenspire is the beating commercial heart of Valdris—a city of waterwheels, warehouses, and smoke-stained brick that never truly sleeps. Stone quays line both banks, groaning under crates of grain, ore, and cloth, while bargemen shout commands in a dozen dialects over the roar of the current. The city's namesake spire is a lone limestone column rising from the river's center, crowned by a lighthouse whose amber beacon guides night traffic through the treacherous gorge. The smell of river mud, tar, and fresh-baked bread from the bakers' guild mingles with the metallic tang of the smithies that cluster near the waterwheels. Humans, halflings, and dwarves rub shoulders on the crowded dockside lanes, and coin changes hands faster than anywhere else in the kingdom. Brothels and counting houses stand side by side, and the City Watch struggles to keep the river pirates and smugglers honest. To stand on the Riven Bridge at dawn and watch the fog burn off the gorge is to understand why merchants say Rivenspire is where Valdris makes its living.
payload.jurisdiction: Governed by the Mayor-Exchequer, an elected official drawn from the Merchant Guild, who oversees civil administration under the Crown's authority. A garrison of Royal Sentries maintains the King's Peace alongside the City Watch.
payload.terrain: River gorge with steep banks, stone quays, and a central limestone spire

payload.summary: Hewn from the living granite of the Frostvein Mountains, the dwarven mountain-hold of Ironhold is less a city than a cathedral of stone—a vast subterranean complex of halls, forges, and galleries that descends seven levels into the earth. The Great Gate, a slab of iron-banded granite twenty feet thick, opens onto a trade-road that winds down into a valley of slag and snow, but beyond it lies a world of vaulted ceilings supported by pillars carved into the shapes of dwarven heroes, lit by basins of eternal forge-fire that cast everything in a warm copper glow. The air is thick with the clang of hammers, the hiss of quenching steel, and the deep, resonant chanting of the Forge-Priests who tend the Everflame. The smell of hot metal, coal smoke, and pickled cave-fish saturates every stone. Dwarves in soot-stained leather aprons trundle ore carts along rails cut into the floor, while children play among the ancestors' statues and elders debate lineage in the mead halls over cups of black stout. Ironhold supplies the kingdom's finest steel and its deepest grudges, and its Thane answers to Crownhaven with a loyalty that is loud, conditional, and grudgingly genuine.
payload.jurisdiction: Ruled by Thain Grimvar Stoneshield, hereditary lord of the Ironhold Clan, who holds his seat by ancient dwarven law and pays tribute to the Crown of Valdris in steel and gold. The Thane's council of guild-masters oversees mining, forging, and defense.
payload.terrain: Subterranean mountain hold carved into granite, seven descending levels, with a single fortified gate

payload.summary: Where the fertile plains of central Valdris give way to the frozen bogs and black pines of the Pale Reach, the garrison town of Northwatch huddles behind its double ring of palisade walls, a hard-edged outpost where the kingdom's northern frontier is held by stubbornness, steel, and badly needed reinforcements. The wind never stops here—it moans through the watch-towers and snaps the royal banner stiff as a board—and snow lies on the ground eight months of the year. Log-and-stone barracks cluster around a central keep of grey granite, their chimneys trailing smoke that smells of pine tar, mutton fat, and the sour tang of cheap ale. Soldiers in fur-lined cloaks patrol the walls with stamping boots and red ears, while trappers, hedge-witches, and the occasional frost-bearded northman come to trade furs and cured meat for iron and salt. The town has been burned and rebuilt three times, and the graveyard is larger than the market square. Every child learns to use a bow before they learn to read, and every door is barred by nightfall. Northwatch is not a place anyone visits for pleasure, but the Knights of the Pale Vow who garrison it are among the most decorated in the realm, and the Crown knows that without them the north would be lost within a season.
payload.jurisdiction: Commanded by the Warden of the Pale Reach, a military governor appointed directly by the Crown of Valdris. Civil authority is subordinate to martial law, and the garrison's Knight-Commander holds the power of summary justice.
payload.terrain: Frozen northern frontier with permafrost bog, black pine forest, and double palisade walls

payload.summary: At the crossroads of the King's Road and the Old Salt Route, where a shallow stone ford crosses the Willowmere Creek, the trade hub of Crossford has grown from a single coaching inn into a sprawling, restless town of merchants, wagoners, and fortune-seekers in barely two generations. The streets are wide and rutted, lined with inns, stables, and storehouses whose signs shout in a babel of languages, and the constant rumble of wagon wheels and clop of hooves gives the whole place the feel of a river in flood. Canvas awnings shade open-air markets where spices from the southern coasts, wool from the highland flocks, and enchanted trinkets from Elfshade change hands amid a din of haggling, laughter, and the occasional shriek of a pickpocket caught by the Watch. The smell of roasting chestnuts, horse dung, and the distinctive pepper-and-clove scent of southern spices mingles over everything. Crossford has no ancient bloodlines or grand architecture—its oldest building is a forty-year-old inn—but it has coin, energy, and a population that doubles during the seasonal fairs. The Merchant Guild's chapterhouse here is the largest outside Rivenspire, and its Master is said to be richer than half the lords of the realm.
payload.jurisdiction: Administered by a Guild-Steward appointed by the Merchant Guild of Rivenspire, confirmed by the Crown's Reeve. A small detachment of Royal Sentries keeps order, but the Guild's own bailiffs handle most commercial disputes.
payload.terrain: Rolling plains at a river ford, crossroads of two major trade routes

payload.summary: Atop the highest hill in Crownhaven, visible for miles across the plains, Sunhelm Keep rises in seven tiers of white limestone and gilded slate—a fortress-palace that is as much a statement of royal power as it is a working seat of government. The outer walls bristle with ballistae and fly the golden dragon banner of Valdris from every tower, but within, the keep opens into sunlit courtyards, marble galleries, and a great throne hall whose vaulted ceiling is painted with the deeds of the kings. Armored Knights of the Crown patrol the corridors in pairs, their crimson cloaks sweeping the flagstones, while scribes, heralds, and petitioners flow through the lower halls in a controlled current of bureaucracy. The air carries wax, old parchment, and the faint perfume of the royal gardens that terrace down the hill's southern face. The King's own guard, the Sunhelms, are quartered in the upper tiers, and their barracks ring with the clash of practice swords from dawn until dusk. Sunhelm Keep has never fallen to siege, and its walls are said to have been blessed by three separate archmages—a claim no enemy has yet dared to test.
payload.jurisdiction: Direct seat of the Crown of Valdris. The King's household and the High Council administer the kingdom from within. The Captain of the Sunhelms commands the royal guard and controls access to the sovereign.
payload.terrain: Fortified hilltop palace with seven tiers, limestone walls, and terraced gardens

payload.summary: The great market square of Crownhaven, known to all as the Gilded Square, is a vast paved plaza at the city's heart where the kingdom's wealth is on daily, noisy, fragrant display. Stalls and pavilions crowd so thickly that the ground disappears beneath canvas, and the alleys between them are barely wide enough for two men to pass shoulder to shoulder. Here a dwarf from Ironhold haggles over a bolt of elven silk beside a Rivenspire factor inspecting a crate of southern spices, while a street conjurer draws a crowd with cantrips and a pie-seller shouts her wares over the din. The air is a layered tapestry of roasting meat, incense, horse sweat, and the sharp green scent of fresh-cut herbs. A bronze fountain at the square's center, shaped like a rearing dragon, spouts clear water that the thirsty and the destitute drink from alike. The City Watch maintains a post at the square's north corner, but the pickpockets and cutpurses treat the crowd as their personal treasury, and a traveler who does not watch their purse will soon be lighter by it.
payload.jurisdiction: Crownhaven civic authority. The Market Master, a royal appointee, regulates stalls, weights, and trade hours. The City Watch maintains a permanent post at the square's north corner.
payload.terrain: Paved open plaza with a central dragon fountain, surrounded by multi-story merchant houses

payload.summary: The Cathedral of the Dawnfire is Crownhaven's spiritual heart, a soaring edifice of white granite and rose-tinted glass that catches the morning sun and sets the entire eastern quarter aglow in shades of amber and rose. Its twin spires, each crowned with a bronze flame that the priests light at every sunrise, can be seen from the city gates, and pilgrims come from across Valdris to touch the Dawnfire Stone—a relic said to have been carried from the heart of a dying star. Inside, the nave is vast and hushed, its floor a mosaic of the cosmos, its columns wrapped in carvings of saints and dragons. The smell of beeswax candles and burning incense hangs thick as a veil, and the chanting of the Dawnfire priesthood rises and falls in a rhythm that seems to slow time itself. Knights who have sworn holy vows kneel in the side chapels, their armor gleaming in the colored light, and the High Priestess herself conducts the Dawnfire Mass each morning to a congregation that spills out into the square. The cathedral also serves as the site of royal coronations, weddings, and funerals, binding the Crown to the Dawnfire faith in a pact older than the kingdom itself.
payload.jurisdiction: Administered by the Order of the Dawnfire, an independent religious hierarchy answerable only to its own High Priestess and, in matters of doctrine, to the Patriarch in the south. The Crown holds the right of nomination for the cathedral's dean but cannot interfere in religious affairs.
payload.terrain: Cathedral complex of white granite with twin spires, rose-glass windows, and a mosaic nave

payload.summary: The Gilded Drake is the most famous tavern in Crownhaven, a four-story timber-and-plaster house on the square's western edge that has been pouring ale since before the city had walls. Its common room is a cavern of dark wood, low beams, and a hearth big enough to roast an ox, around which travelers, sellswords, off-duty guardsmen, and the occasional disguised noble gather on benches worn smooth by generations of backsides. The air is a warm fog of pipe smoke, spilled ale, mutton grease, and the distinctly human smell of too many bodies in too little space. A bard in the corner competes with the roar of conversation, and the barkeep—a mountain of a woman named Hesta who remembers every face and every tab—presides over the tap with the authority of a general. Rooms upstairs range from a straw mattress in a shared loft to a private chamber with a lock and a window, and the quality of the clientele rises with the floor. Rumors are the Gilded Drake's true currency, and more plots, alliances, and betrayals have been hatched over its tables than in half the council chambers of Valdris.
payload.jurisdiction: A private establishment licensed by the Crownhaven civic authority. Hesta Ironhand, the proprietor, holds the license and enforces her own form of justice—troublemakers are ejected physically and banned permanently.
payload.terrain: Four-story timber tavern on the edge of the Gilded Square, with a large common room and a central hearth

entries.name: The Watchtower of the Iron Gate

payload.summary: The Watchtower of the Iron Gate is the headquarters of the Crownhaven City Watch, a squat, iron-banded fortress of dark stone set into the city's main gatehouse, from which the Watch's captain commands a force of three hundred armsmen responsible for keeping order in the capital. The tower bristles with alarm bells, signal fires, and a gryphon-weathered mast from which the Watch's black-and-gold pennant flies day and night. Inside, the ground floor is a mustering hall where shifts are briefed over maps of the city's districts, its walls hung with wanted posters and chalkboards tracking crime patterns. The air smells of leather, lamp oil, and the sweat of men who have walked a long patrol. Cells in the basement hold the night's catch—drunkards, pickpockets, and the occasional murderer—awaiting the morning magistrate. The Watch is widely considered underfunded and overstretched, but its captain, a scarred veteran named Doran Black, is feared by the criminal element and respected by the Crown, and under his command the capital's streets are safer than those of any other city in the kingdom.
payload.jurisdiction: The City Watch answers to the Mayor of Crownhaven, who is appointed by the Crown. Captain Doran Black commands day-to-day operations and holds the authority to detain, charge, and present accused persons before the royal magistrate.
payload.terrain: Fortified gatehouse tower with mustering hall, armory, and holding cells

payload.summary: At the peak of Dragonrest's mountain fortress, accessible only by a spiraling staircase cut into the cliff face and defended by three murder-holes and a portcullis of solid iron, sits the Wyrmstone Throne—the seat of the Warden of Dragonrest and the command center from which the mountain fortress is directed. The throne chamber is a natural cavern expanded by dwarven masons into a vaulted hall of black basalt, its walls veined with a strange green mineral that glows faintly in the dark. The throne itself is carved from a single block of green-veined stone said to have been a dragon's resting place, and it is from this that the fortress takes its name. The air is cold and mineral, carrying the distant rumble of subterranean rivers. Maps of the mountain passes cover every table, and a war-council is perpetually in session, for Dragonrest guards the kingdom's most vulnerable highland approach. The Warden's personal guard, the Wyrmstone Sentinels, stand at eternal attention in armor of black steel, and their stillness is so complete that visitors sometimes mistake them for statues until one shifts his weight and the armor whispers against itself.
payload.jurisdiction: The Warden of Dragonrest, appointed by the Crown of Valdris, holds absolute military authority over the fortress and its garrison. The Warden commands the Wyrmstone Sentinels and the mountain garrison, and answers directly to the King.
payload.terrain: Mountain-peak cavern hall of black basalt with green-veined glowing mineral, accessible only by cliff staircase

payload.summary: Beneath Dragonrest, in a cavern heated by a natural volcanic vent, the Emberforge burns with a fire that has not been extinguished in four hundred years—a furnace of dwarven design tended by a brotherhood of smiths who are equal parts artisans, priests, and soldiers. The cavern is a cathedral of fire and metal: massive anvils sit on stone platforms around the central furnace, and the walls are hung with finished blades, pikes, and plate armor that gleam in the ember-light. The heat is staggering, the air shimmering and thick with the smell of coal, hot iron, and the acrid bite of quenching oil. The forge-smiths work in leather aprons and nothing else, their bare arms glistening, and they speak little, communicating through the rhythm of their hammers—a language said to be understood only by the steel. The Emberforge produces the finest weapons in Dragonrest's arsenal, including the signature black-steel blades of the Wyrmstone Sentinels, and its master smith, a grizzled dwarf named Brogar Ashhand, is rumored to know the secret of forging dragonbone into steel—a secret he will take to his grave.
payload.jurisdiction: The Emberforge is an autonomous guild under the authority of the Warden of Dragonrest. Master Smith Brogar Ashhand governs the brotherhood and controls all production, which is dedicated to the fortress garrison and the Crown's commission.
payload.terrain: Underground volcanic forge cavern with a perpetual furnace, stone platforms, and weapon-lined walls

payload.summary: At the very top of Dragonrest's highest tower, open to the wind and the weather through a great stone latticework, the High Rookery is home to the fortress's messenger ravens—a flock of three hundred black birds bred, trained, and enchanted by the fortress's Master of Wings to carry intelligence between Dragonrest, Crownhaven, Northwatch, and every outpost in between. The rookery is a wind-swept, guano-scented chamber of wooden perches, nesting boxes, and a great central roost where the Master of Wings, a wiry old ranger named Tella Windvoice, spends her days among the birds. The ravens are not ordinary corvids—each is bound by a minor enchantment that allows it to memorize a message and repeat it flawlessly to the designated recipient, and they are loyal to the Crown alone. The floor is a carpet of feathers and dropped scraps, and the constant croaking of the birds forms a kind of ambient music that Tella claims she can read for omens. On clear days, the view from the rookery spans the entire mountain range, and it is said that nothing moves in the high passes that Tella's ravens do not see and report.
payload.jurisdiction: The High Rookery is under the direct authority of the Warden of Dragonrest. Master of Wings Tella Windvoice commands the raven flock and controls all intelligence traffic, reporting directly to the Warden and, in emergencies, to the Crown.
payload.terrain: Open-air tower rookery at the fortress peak, with stone latticework, wooden perches, and panoramic mountain views

entries.name: The Chapel of the Veiled Flame

payload.summary: Carved into a quiet ledge of the fortress's inner wall, the Chapel of the Veiled Flame is Dragonrest's place of worship—a small, solemn space of grey stone and dim light where the garrison's soldiers come to pray before battle and to honor their dead. A single altar of polished obsidian holds the Veiled Flame, a fire that burns without fuel or smoke behind a screen of thin alabaster, casting a soft, steady light that is said to soothe troubled hearts and grant courage to the faithful. The walls are carved with the names of every soldier who has died in the fortress's defense, a list that grows longer with every generation, and the air smells of cold stone, burnt offerings, and the faint sweetness of dried flowers laid at the altar by widows and orphans. A single chaplain, an aging knight who took holy orders after losing his sword-arm, tends the flame and offers counsel, and his voice is the only one that ever breaks the chapel's heavy silence. The Veiled Flame is the only light in Dragonrest that never goes out, and the garrison believes that if it ever does, the fortress will fall within the year.
payload.jurisdiction: The Chapel of the Veiled Flame is an independent religious house under the loose authority of the Order of the Dawnfire, though it follows a martial tradition distinct from the capital's cathedral.
