The floor is sand covered with woven mats, and the students — girls and boys from every island, chosen for memory and sea-sense and sent as children to serve a ten-year bond — sit in rows before the masters, chanting the star-path songs in call-and-response, their voices rising and falling in the complex melodies that encode the navigation knowledge: the rising-points and setting-points of the guide-stars, the swell-directions of the great ocean currents, the bird-flight patterns that signal land, the cloud-signs of islands beyond the horizon. The walls are hung with star-charts painted on bark-cloth and with the carved staffs of past masters, each notched with the voyages of its holder, and a great navigation-circle of stones and sticks occupies the hall's center, used to teach the star-compass — the mental diagram of thirty-two points by which a wayfinder orients the rising and setting of every star. The air smells of sand, palm, green tea, and the faint sweat of concentration. The Star-Father, a grey-haired man with milk-pale eyes from years of night-watching, presides and corrects, his voice quiet but carrying over the chant.
payload.jurisdiction: Under the Wayfinder's Circle and the Star-Father. The school is the heart of the island's authority; all training, curriculum, and graduation are decided here. No one may teach the wayfinder's art outside the school's sanction, and the unlicensed claiming of wayfinder-status is a grave offense punished across the archipelago.
payload.terrain: open-sided hardwood hall, sand-mat floor, central navigation-circle, bark-cloth star-charts

payload.summary: The Star Stones are the great navigation-circle of Hokuala, a permanent ring of standing stones set in the sand of the island's highest point — a low dune barely above the palm-tops but the only spot on the flat atoll with an unbroken view of the horizon in every direction. Thirty-two stones, each waist-high and carved with the face of its star, stand in a circle around a central stone that marks the navigator's stance, and the sand between them is raked smooth each evening so that the master can lay out the swell-patterns and current-directions in sticks and shells, teaching the students to read the whole ocean from a single point. The stones are black basalt brought from Motu Peleki and Makapaa, each hauled across the sea and set by the joint labor of the archipelago's islands as an offering to the wayfinder's art, and they are sacred — touched only by masters and graduating students, who lay their hands on their birth-star stone as they receive their navigator's staff. By night the circle is the island's observatory, the masters and senior students standing within it reading the stars through the carved sighting-grooves on each stone, their voices low as they confirm the star-paths and track the slow drift of the guide-stars through the seasons. The wind is constant here at the dune-top, and the air smells of salt and sand and the cold clarity of the open sky.
payload.jurisdiction: Sacred ground under the Wayfinder's Circle. The stones may be touched only by masters and graduating students, and the circle may not be entered by the uninitiated except by the Star-Father's leave. Damage to a stone is an archipelago-wide offense, as each was gifted by an island.
payload.terrain: dune-top standing-stone circle, raked sand, carved sighting-grooves, open horizon view

payload.summary: The Student Dormitory is the living-quarters of Hokuala, a long low building of palm-thatch and woven-reed walls on the lagoon-shore near the school, divided into sleeping-bays of woven mats on a raised sand floor where the students — some forty children and youths at any time — sleep, eat, and keep their few possessions. The bays are communal, eight to a side, each with a small carved cubby for personal things and a hook for the wrap that is each student's only garment, and the air is close and warm with the smell of young bodies, salt, palm-fibre mats, and the green tea that is always brewing on the dormitory's small cook-hearth. The students rise before dawn for the first star-watch, train through the morning on the lagoon, attend the school in the heat of the day, and return to the star-stones or the lagoon at dusk, so the dormitory is busiest at midday rest and in the brief hours of sleep, when the chant of the star-path songs can be heard muttered by students drilling in their mats even in their dreams. A dormitory-elder, a senior student in the last year of training, keeps order and rouses the sleepers, and the walls are hung with the students' practice star-charts, drawn and redrawn in charcoal on bark-paper, the evidence of years of learning.
payload.jurisdiction: Under the dormitory-elder, a senior student appointed by the Wayfinder's Circle, with the Star-Father's oversight. Discipline is strict — laziness, dishonesty, or a broken focus-rule can mean expulsion, and the wayfinder's art admits no half-mastery.
payload.terrain: palm-thatch dormitory, reed walls, sand-floor mat-bays, cook-hearth

payload.summary: The Training Canoe House is the boat-shed of Hokuala, a long open-fronted hall of hardwood and palm-thatch on the lagoon-shore where the training-canoes are kept — small outriggers built light for single-student sailing, each fitted with a miniature sail and a star-compass mark painted on the bow for the student to orient by. The canoes are racked on driftwood stands in rows, their hulls scraped and re-painted each season, and the shed smells of wood-shavings, fresh paint, tar, and the salt-damp of the lagoon. A boat-master, a retired wayfinder who lost his sea-legs to age but not his eye, builds and maintains the training-canoes here with two apprentices, and he also oversees the practical sailing-exercises that are the core of the training: each student must solo a training-canoe from the lagoon to a marked point beyond the reef and back, by star and swell alone, before they are allowed near a true voyaging-canoe. The shed's back wall holds the graduated staffs of every wayfinder trained here, each carved with their name and graduating voyage, a record stretching back generations, and the students touch the wall for luck before each solo exercise. The lagoon is visible through the open front, its water bright and shallow, the reef-edge marked by the line of breaking white where the training-ground begins.
payload.jurisdiction: Under the boat-master, whose authority over the canoe-house and the training-canoes is ratified by the Wayfinder's Circle. He controls canoe assignment, maintenance, and the scheduling of solo exercises, and may ground a student for unsafe sailing.
payload.terrain: open-fronted hardwood boat-shed, lagoon-shore, canoe racks, reef-edge training-ground

payload.summary: The Sky-Reading Platform is the night-observatory of Hokuala, a raised platform of hardwood poles and split bamboo built on the island's eastern shore where the reef falls away into deep water and the horizon is dark and clear, used by the masters and senior students for the night-watches that are the final and most demanding phase of wayfinder training. The platform is open to the sky, its only shelter a low wind-screen of woven palm, and its floor is strewn with woven mats where the watchers lie on their backs and read the stars — the rising and setting of the guide-stars, the slow arc of the sea-stars that mark the seasons, the phosphorescent wakes of the deep-water currents that a master can read as a second compass in the dark sea below. The air at night is cold for the tropics, salt and clear, and the silence is deep, broken only by the lap of the reef and the low murmur of a master naming a star to a student or correcting a sighting. A small clay fire-pot on the platform's edge holds a smouldering ember for warmth and for the green tea brewed through the long watches, and the students learn here to read the sky without instruments — by eye, memory, and the song-magic that binds the star-paths into a single mental map of the voyaging-world. It is here, on a clear night at the turn of the season, that a graduating student makes their vigil — a night alone on the platform, reading every star and swell, to prove they are ready for their first true voyage.
payload.jurisdiction: Under the Wayfinder's Circle. The platform is reserved for masters and senior students except during the graduation vigil. Silence is the only rule here, and to speak loudly on the platform during a night-watch is a grave breach punished by extra duties.
payload.terrain: raised hardwood observation platform, eastern deep-water shore, open sky, wind-screen

payload.summary: Motu Lotu is the refuge-island of the Tide Archipelago, a low sandy motu on the archipelago's windward edge that has become the gathering-place for the islanders displaced by the rising seas that are slowly drowning the outer atolls — families whose home-islands have been swallowed by the waves, fishermen whose reefs have gone dead, whole clans who arrived with nothing but the canoes they fled in. The island itself is unprepossessing — a crescent of white sand with a thin fringe of wind-bent palms and a single brackish well — but it has been built up with a sprawling camp of shelters of driftwood, palm-thatch, and salvaged canoe-sail, their walls patched with bark-cloth and matting, stretching along the crescent beach and inland among the palms in a dense, improvised warren of lanes and compounds that grows every season as more boats arrive. The sound of Motu Lotu is unlike any other island — not the settled hum of a village but a shifting chorus of many island dialects, the crying of infants, the low voices of elders telling the stories of drowned homes, and the constant work of building, patching, and preparing. The smell is of salt, damp thatch, cook-smoke, and the faint undertone of grief that no wind fully carries away. The people here are hospitable to a fault — they have known loss — and they share what little they have, but the question that hangs over every fire is the same: where will we go when this island too goes under.
payload.jurisdiction: Governed by the Camp-Council, an elected body of representatives from each displaced clan-community, chaired by a Camp-Mother or Camp-Father chosen by the council to serve a one-year term. The Camp-Council allocates shelter-sites, manages the well-water rationing, mediates between clans, and coordinates with Lani Atoll's Tide-Moot, which claims protectorate authority and sends aid — food, water, cordage — but rarely intervenes directly.
payload.terrain: low sand motu, palm fringe, brackish well, sprawling driftwood-and-thatch camp

payload.summary: The Welcome Longhouse is the intake-hall of Motu Lotu, the first structure a new arrival sees — a long open-sided building of driftwood and palm-thatch at the camp's landward end, built on the highest ground so that a canoe approaching the island sees its roof first, a signal that this is a place of refuge. Inside, the Camp-Council's welcomers — a rotation of elder women who have themselves been refugees — receive each new family or lone arrival, recording their names, their home-island, and their needs on bark-paper tallies, and assigning them a shelter-site and a clan-community to join. A cook-hearth at the hall's center always has a pot of fish-stew simmering, and every new arrival is fed before any other business, a tradition the camp holds sacred — no one is turned away hungry. The walls are hung with the carved name-boards of the drowned islands, each carved by a survivor with the island's name and the date it was lost, and the welcomers lay a hand on the relevant board as they record a new arrival's origin, a gesture of witness. The air smells of wood-smoke, fish-stew, salt, and the green tea that is always brewing. A small shrine to the sea-spirit stands at the hall's corner, where new arrivals are invited to make an offering of thanks for safe arrival and to mourn what the sea has taken.
payload.jurisdiction: Under the Camp-Council's welcomers, directed by the Camp-Mother. The Welcome Longhouse is the camp's official entry-point; no one may settle in the camp without registering here. The welcomers have authority to assign shelter-sites and clan-community affiliation, and to refer cases of conflict or special need to the full council.
payload.terrain: open-sided driftwood longhouse, cook-hearth, carved name-board walls, corner shrine

payload.summary: The Shelter Rows are the residential heart of Motu Lotu, the dense warren of driftwood-and-thatch shelters that stretches along the crescent beach and inland among the palms, each shelter a small compound of one or two sleeping-huts and a cook-space, walled with woven palm and patched with sail-cloth, bark-cloth, and whatever a family has salvaged or bartered. The lanes between them are sand, swept clean by each household and marked with shells and stones to show the boundary, and the rows are organized loosely by clan-community, each cluster flying the signal-cloth of its home-island from a high pole so that a new arrival can find their own people. The shelters are built close for wind-shelter and for the comfort of neighbors, and the sound of the rows is of children playing, women talking across the lane-walls, the rhythmic thud of breadfruit being pounded, and the low chanting of elders teaching the old songs to children who will never see the islands they describe. The smell is of cook-smoke, thatch, salt, and the sweet rot of palm-husks composting in the small garden-patches where each household grows a few taro and sweet-potato in the poor sand, supplemented by the fish caught from the reef. A lane-elder, chosen by each cluster, keeps the peace and reports needs to the Camp-Council, and the rows are rebuilt and extended constantly as new arrivals come and old shelters rot in the salt air.
payload.jurisdiction: Shelter-sites are allotted by the Camp-Council through the welcomers, and each household holds its site by use-right so long as it maintains the shelter and contributes to camp labor. Lane-elders settle routine neighbor disputes; serious cases go to the Camp-Council. No site may be sold or permanently enclosed.
payload.terrain: sand-lane driftwood-and-thatch compound warren, shell-marked boundaries, garden-patches

payload.summary: The Healing Canopy is the medicine-house of Motu Lotu, a large open-sided shelter of driftwood poles and a great sail-cloth awning stretched between the palms at the camp's center, where the camp's healers — a council of women and men from a dozen islands, each carrying the herbal and spiritual medicine of their home — tend the sick, the injured, and the grief-wounded who are the camp's particular affliction. The floor is sand covered with woven mats, and the space is divided by hung bark-cloth curtains into treatment-bays where the healers work: brewing herbal decoctions in clay pots on small hearths, setting broken bones with bamboo splints, suturing wounds with bone needles and fibre-thread, and — most often and most needed — sitting with the grief-stricken, the refugees who have lost homes and family to the sea, singing the comfort-songs and administering the calming brews that are the healers' particular skill. The air smells of green herbs, wood-smoke, the bitter tang of medicinal decoctions, and the clean salt of the sea-wind that flows through the open sides. Bundles of dried herbs hang from the awling-poles — gathered from the surviving islands and sent as aid — and a small spirit-corner holds offerings to the healing-spirits and the sea-spirit, whose anger the healers say must be acknowledged before grief can ease. The chief healer, a quiet woman from a drowned atoll, coordinates the council and trains apprentices from among the camp's youth.
payload.jurisdiction: Under the chief healer and the healing-council, independent of the Camp-Council in matters of treatment. The healers may quarantine the sick, compel rest, and forbid labor on medical grounds, and their authority is respected by all. The Healing Canopy is neutral ground; no dispute may be pursued within it.
payload.terrain: open-sided sail-cloth canopy, sand-mat floor, bark-cloth treatment-bays, herb-hung poles

payload.summary: The Shared Cookfire is the communal kitchen and gathering-place of Motu Lotu, a broad sand clearing at the camp's center ringed with driftwood logs for seats and dominated by a row of earth-ovens — pits lined with heated stones and banana leaves — where the camp's daily meals are cooked collectively, each household contributing fish or produce to a shared pot and receiving back a share scaled to its size. The cookfire is tended by a rotation of camp-wide volunteers overseen by the Fire-Mother, a formidable elder who controls the ovens and the food-ration with an exact sense of fairness, and the smell of roasting fish, breadfruit, and taro hangs over the clearing from dawn to dusk, the smoke drifting through the palms in blue threads. The Shared Cookfire is also the camp's social heart — the place where news is exchanged, where the Camp-Council makes announcements, where the elders tell the old stories of the drowned islands in the evenings so that the children remember, and where the musicians — refugees who brought their instruments and their songs — play the nose-flute and the slit-drum while the camp sings the songs of a dozen islands, some mournful, some joyful, all carrying the weight of what was lost. At night the firelight turns the clearing amber, and the gathered camp — many islands, many clans, one people now — eats together and the sound of their voices is like the sea.
payload.jurisdiction: Under the Fire-Mother, appointed by the Camp-Council. She controls the earth-ovens, the food-rotation, and the ration-shares, and her fairness is the camp's trust. The Shared Cookfire is communal ground; no household may claim a permanent seat or a larger share than its number warrants.
payload.terrain: central sand clearing, earth-oven pits, driftwood-log seats, firelit gathering-space

payload.summary: The Memorial Driftwood is the sacred place of Motu Lotu, a great stand of driftwood logs — some as thick as a man's body, bleached bone-white by sun and salt — set upright in the sand at the camp's windward edge where the beach faces the open sea and the drowned islands beyond. Each log is carved with the name of a lost island, the date of its drowning, and the names of the dead who did not escape, the carving done by survivors with shell-adzes and obsidian blades, the letters filled with charcoal and resin so they stand black against the white wood. New logs are added as new islands fall, and the stand has grown from a handful to a small forest of pale pillars that creak and sway in the wind, hung with offerings of flowers, shell-leis, and the small carved figures of the ancestors the drowned islands honored. At every new moon the camp gathers here in silence as the sea-shaman — a refugee from the first drowned atoll — chants the names of the lost islands and pours an offering of fresh water and palm-wine into the sea, asking the sea-spirit to remember the dead and to spare the living a little longer. The air at the Memorial is always quieter than the rest of the camp, the wind hushed by the logs, and the sand at their base is strewn with the faded leis of past ceremonies. It is the camp's most sacred ground, and no one passes it without pausing, and no child plays here.
payload.jurisdiction: Sacred ground under the sea-shaman and the Camp-Council jointly. The Memorial may not be built upon, quarreled over, or entered except for ceremony or private mourning. To deface a memorial-log is the camp's gravest offense, punished by permanent expulsion.
payload.terrain: windward beach, upright bleached driftwood pillars, carved memorial-logs, offering-strewn sand

payload.summary: The Conch-Chief's Hall is the seat of Lani Atoll's governance and the meeting-place of the Tide-Moot, the great council of the archipelago's island-chiefs, built on the atoll's highest ground — a great mound of sand and coral-stone raised by generations of chiefs to lift the hall above the highest storm-tide. The hall is a great open-sided building of hardwood and palm-thatch, its roof sweeping low at the eaves and rising to a high ridge-pole carved with the coiled forms of octopus and sea-serpent and painted in black, red, and white, its pillars carved with the figures of past chiefs and hung with the great conch-shell trumpets that give the hall its name. The Tide-Moot meets here at the turn of every season, the island-chiefs and elders gathering from across the archipelago to decide the affairs of the nation — war and peace, the allotment of fishing-grounds, the aid due to islands threatened by the rising seas, the disputes that cannot be settled locally — and the Conch-Chief of Lani Atoll, the first among equals, presides from a raised seat of polished coral-stone draped with tapa-cloth, the speaking-staff of carved whale-bone in hand. The floor is sand covered with fine woven mats, and the walls are hung with the tribute and record of the archipelago — feather-work, obsidian blades, shell-wealth, and the bark-paper tallies of every Moot going back generations. The air smells of salt, palm, woodsmoke from the central hearth, and the kava-root brew that is served to every chief at Moot. A great conch hangs by the Conch-Chief's seat, blown only to open and close the Moot.
payload.jurisdiction: Seat of the Conch-Chief of Lani Atoll and the Tide-Moot of the whole archipelago. The Conch-Chief is chosen from the chiefs of Lani Atoll's clans by ritual contest and holds the first-voice at Moot but not a veto. The hall and its mound are sovereign ground; no chief may draw a weapon here under pain of the whole archipelago's sanction.
payload.terrain: raised sand-and-coral mound, open-sided hardwood hall, carved pillars, central hearth

payload.summary: The Great Canoe Shed is the boat-house of Lani Atoll, a long cathedral-like structure of hardwood and palm-thatch on the lagoon-shore where the archipelago's great voyaging canoes — the double-hulled vessels that carry fifty sailors and trade-goods across hundreds of leagues of open sea — are housed, repaired, and built. The shed is vast, its ridge-pole higher than a man's height doubled to fit the prows of the great canoes, and its floor is sand swept clean and strewn with wood-shavings, the smell of fresh-cut hardwood, tar, and the sweet sandalwood used for the finest prows filling the air. Three or four great canoes rest on cradles of driftwood at any time — some newly building, some being re-caulked and re-rigged, some resting between voyages — their hulls of sewn plank painted black and red with staring eye-prows at the bow to ward off sea-spirits, their twin masts stepped and their great sails of woven pandanus folded and stored in cedar chests along the wall. The master canoe-builder, a quiet man with hands scarred from a lifetime of adze-work, oversees a crew of shipwrights and apprentices, and the shed is the island's pride: a new voyaging-canoe, launched with ceremony and sung across the sea by a wayfinder from Hokuala, is an event the whole archipelago marks. Tools — adzes, caulking-mallets, bone drills — hang on the walls, and the cordage comes fresh from Vanua Tafola's works.
payload.jurisdiction: Under the master canoe-builder, whose authority over the shed is ratified by the Conch-Chief. He controls canoe-building, repair, and launching, and the apprenticeship system. The Great Canoe Shed is a place of craft-pride; sabotage of a canoe is a capital offense against the archipelago.
payload.terrain: lagoon-shore boat-shed, sand floor, voyaging-canoe cradles, tool-hung walls

payload.summary: The Singing Grotto is the sacred heart of Lani Atoll, a sea-cave beneath the island's windward shore reached by a descending path of coral-stone steps that drops below the tide-line into a hidden chamber where the roof is pierced by a natural shaft and the walls are carved — by hands far older than the archipelago's memory — with spirals, wave-patterns, and the staring faces of sea-spirits in a style no living carver can replicate. The grotto's floor is a pool of sea-water that rises and falls with the tide, and the chamber's acoustics are its wonder: any sound made here is caught and multiplied by the carved walls and the shaft, so that a single voice becomes a choir, a chant becomes a harmony of echoes, and the wayfinding song-magic — the star-path songs that the masters of Hokuala teach — resonates here with a power and clarity found nowhere else. The island's spirit-shaman, a woman of great age who is said to have sung in the grotto since before the first chief, conducts the highest rites of the song-magic here: the binding of a master-wayfinder's spirit to the sea and the stars, the blessing of a new voyaging-canoe, and the Great Singing at the turn of the year, when the whole island gathers on the steps above and the shaman sings the archipelago into being again, her voice rising from the grotto in a cascade of harmony that is said to reach the sea-spirit and the star-spirits alike. The air is cold, wet, salt, and charged, and the carved faces seem to move in the lamplight.
payload.jurisdiction: Sovereign under the spirit-shaman, independent of the Conch-Chief and the Tide-Moot in all matters of spirit and song-magic. The grotto is the archipelago's most sacred site; entry is by the shaman's leave only, and the highest rites are witnessed only by the initiated. To carve or mark the ancient walls is an unthinkable sacrilege.
payload.terrain: sub-tidal sea-cave, natural skylight shaft, carved spirit-walls, resonant tidal pool

entries.name: The Feast Ground of the Full Moon

payload.summary: The Feast Ground of the Full Moon is the great gathering-place of Lani Atoll, a broad open clearing of swept sand inland from the chief's hall, ringed by breadfruit and coconut palms and dominated at its center by a great earth-oven complex — a row of stone-lined pits that can cook for hundreds — and a raised platform of coral-stone and driftwood where the drummers and chanters perform. Every full moon the whole island gathers here for the feast that is the atoll's chief ceremony and its joy: the earth-ovens are fired before dawn, the day is given to cooking and preparation, and at dusk the drums begin and the people gather, the chiefs in their feather-cloaks, the families with their children, the elders with their carved staves, and the feast is shared — roast pig and breadfruit, taro-pudding wrapped in banana leaves, fish in coconut cream, fermented breadfruit paste, and the kava and palm-wine that flow freely. The drummers on the platform play the complex polyrhythms that drive the dance, and the dancers — men and women in bark-cloth and shell-adornment — perform the story-dances of the archipelago, the voyaging, the fishing, the rising seas, the drowning of the outer islands, the finding of refuge, their bodies telling in movement what the songs tell in word. The firelight turns the clearing gold, the smoke rises through the palms, and the sound of drum and chant and laughter carries out over the lagoon. It is the heart of the archipelago's shared life, and the full-moon feasts draw visitors from every island.
payload.jurisdiction: Common ground managed by the Feast-Master, appointed by the Conch-Chief. The Feast-Master coordinates the full-moon feasts, the earth-ovens, and the performance-platform, and arbitrates the informal precedence of chiefs and clans at the gathering. The Feast Ground may not be built upon; it is held in perpetuity for the gathering.
payload.terrain: swept-sand clearing, palm-ring, earth-oven pits, coral-stone performance platform

payload.summary: The Tattoo Hut is the ritual-house of Lani Atoll, a small dark hut of woven palm and hardwood set apart at the edge of the feast-ground, where the island's tattoo-master — a hereditary office held by a lineage said to have been taught the art by the sea-spirit itself — marks the bodies of the islanders with the spirals, waves, and sea-creature designs that record a person's lineage, deeds, and spirit-pacts, and that are the visible language of status and identity across the archipelago. The work is done with bone-comb mallets dipped in the ink of soot and candlenut-oil, tapped into the skin in long painful sessions, and the hut's air is thick with the smell of the oil, the green leaves chewed for pain, and the faint salt-metal scent of blood — a sacred smell, the tattoo-master says, for the marking is a sacrifice to the spirit that owns the design. The hut's walls are hung with the bone-combs of the lineage, each carved by its master, and the pattern-boards — painted bark-cloth showing the great designs — that a client may choose from or that the master may prescribe by right of lineage. A youth receives their first marking at coming-of-age, a voyager is marked for each great voyage, a chief for each Moot they preside over, and the master alone may add to or refuse a design, reading a person's right to a mark in the spirit-omens. The drum-beat of the mallet carries from the hut, and the islanders say a person is not truly of the sea until they have been marked.
payload.jurisdiction: Sovereign under the tattoo-master, whose authority over marking is absolute and independent of the Conch-Chief. He alone may grant, refuse, or prescribe a design, and to wear an ungranted mark is a grave offense punished by the master's cutting it out and the island's shunning. The Tattoo Hut is inviolate; no one may interrupt a marking session.
payload.terrain: woven-palm ritual hut, bone-comb tools, pattern-board walls, marking-bench

payload.summary: A strip of churned earth, broken stone walls, and old trenches between Valdris's southern hills and Verdania's northern canopy. Called "No Man's Land" by the soldiers who die in it. The mud is grey and deep, the craters fill with rain, and neither side has gained meaningful ground in a generation. It smells of wet earth, rusted iron, and something sweeter underneath -- the Verdanian jungle creeping north, one root at a time.
payload.jurisdiction: Contested between the Kingdom of Valdris (Verdmarch Constabulary) and Verdania (Wardens of the Briar). Neither side holds it fully.
payload.terrain: churned earth, broken stone walls, old trenches, grey mud, rain-filled craters, creeping jungle edge

payload.summary: A stone tower on the Valdrian side, garrisoned by the Field Constabulary. Half-crumbled, rebuilt, half-crumbled again. The banner of the crowned iron tower hangs from the highest remaining wall.
payload.jurisdiction: Contested between the Kingdom of Valdris (Verdmarch Constabulary) and Verdania (Wardens of the Briar). Neither side holds it fully.
payload.terrain: stone tower, crumbled masonry, garrisoned battlement

payload.summary: A muddy camp of canvas tents and cookfires behind the Valdrian trench line. Soldiers play dice, sharpen blades, and watch the treeline. The officers' tent has a table map pinned with iron markers.
payload.jurisdiction: Contested between the Kingdom of Valdris (Verdmarch Constabulary) and Verdania (Wardens of the Briar). Neither side holds it fully.
payload.terrain: canvas tents, cookfires, muddy ground, trench-line rear

payload.summary: A network of deep trenches dug into the grey clay, reinforced with timber and iron. They flood in rain. The walls are carved with names, tallies, and prayers. The mud at the bottom smells like old blood.
payload.jurisdiction: Contested between the Kingdom of Valdris (Verdmarch Constabulary) and Verdania (Wardens of the Briar). Neither side holds it fully.
payload.terrain: deep trenches, grey clay, timber and iron reinforcement, flood-prone

payload.summary: On the Verdanian side, a wall of living thorns and deadfalls maintained by the Wardens of the Briar. The thorns are as thick as a man's finger and grow back faster than they can be cut. Bodies left in the briar are not retrieved.
payload.jurisdiction: Contested between the Kingdom of Valdris (Verdmarch Constabulary) and Verdania (Wardens of the Briar). Neither side holds it fully.
payload.terrain: living thorn wall, deadfalls, jungle edge, Verdanian side

payload.summary: The only overland route between Sangguo and Al-Khayzar -- a narrow canyon through red rock mountains, hot enough to kill a man at midday. Caravans move through in the cool hours: spice and saffron going north, silk and lacquer going south. Toll stations at both ends take their cut. Bandits hide in the side-gorges where the canyon narrows to single-file width. The rock walls are scarved with graffiti in a dozen languages, some of them dead.
payload.jurisdiction: Jointly administered by Sangguo's western prefecture and Al-Khayzar's northern caravan guild. Both collect tolls.
payload.terrain: narrow canyon, red rock mountains, blistering midday heat, side-gorges, carved graffiti

payload.summary: A stone customs house at the Sangguo end of the pass, where officials inspect cargo and collect tolls. The courtyard has space for a dozen wagons. The officials are thorough and slow.
payload.jurisdiction: Jointly administered by Sangguo's western prefecture and Al-Khayzar's northern caravan guild. Both collect tolls.
payload.terrain: stone customs house, wagon courtyard, canyon mouth

payload.summary: A caravanserai at the Al-Khayzar end, with a deep well, shaded arcades, and a stable for camels. The toll collector here is said to take a personal cut on top of the official rate.
payload.jurisdiction: Jointly administered by Sangguo's western prefecture and Al-Khayzar's northern caravan guild. Both collect tolls.
payload.terrain: caravanserai, deep well, shaded arcades, camel stable

payload.summary: The tightest section of the pass, where the canyon walls close to shoulder width for a hundred yards. Rockfalls are common. Bandits drop stones and rope from above. The walls are carved with prayers in old scripts.
payload.jurisdiction: Jointly administered by Sangguo's western prefecture and Al-Khayzar's northern caravan guild. Both collect tolls.
payload.terrain: shoulder-width canyon, rockfall-prone, vertical walls, carved prayers

payload.summary: A maze of narrow side-canyons that branch off the main pass. Some lead to hidden springs. Some lead to bandit camps. Some lead nowhere. The light inside is red and strange.
payload.jurisdiction: Jointly administered by Sangguo's western prefecture and Al-Khayzar's northern caravan guild. Both collect tolls.
payload.terrain: maze of narrow side-canyons, hidden springs, red strange light

payload.summary: A chain of jagged, ice-slicked sea-rocks and broken islands in the strait between Hrafnland's southern coast and Valdris's northern shore. The skerries are navigable only by shallow-draft vessels, which favors Hrafnland longships. In winter the rocks freeze solid and the passage becomes a death trap of black ice and grinding floes. Both nations claim fishing rights. The rocks are unnamed on most maps because the people who survive them are too superstitious to name them.
payload.jurisdiction: Contested between the Kingdom of Valdris (Northwatch garrison) and Hrafnland (jarls of the southern fjords). Fishing rights are disputed; passage rights are enforced by whoever has more ships.
payload.terrain: jagged ice-slicked sea-rocks, broken islands, shallow-draft passages, winter black ice, grinding floes

payload.summary: The largest skerry, flat enough for a dozen tents and a signal fire. Hrafnland raiders use it as a waystation. There is a shallow cave with a hearth and marks on the wall counting the ships that have passed.
payload.jurisdiction: Contested between the Kingdom of Valdris (Northwatch garrison) and Hrafnland (jarls of the southern fjords). Fishing rights are disputed; passage rights are enforced by whoever has more ships.
payload.terrain: large flat skerry, shallow cave, signal-fire site, waystation

payload.summary: A cluster of rocks where at least three ships have gone down. The wreckage is visible at low tide -- timber, iron, and the bones of sailors no one came for. Fish are plentiful here, which is why boats still come.
payload.jurisdiction: Contested between the Kingdom of Valdris (Northwatch garrison) and Hrafnland (jarls of the southern fjords). Fishing rights are disputed; passage rights are enforced by whoever has more ships.
payload.terrain: wreck-cluster rocks, low-tide wreckage, plentiful fish, sailor bones

payload.summary: The passage between the two largest skerries, where the current is fastest and the ice forms first. A longship can pass at speed. Anything wider cannot. The ice groans like something alive.
payload.jurisdiction: Contested between the Kingdom of Valdris (Northwatch garrison) and Hrafnland (jarls of the southern fjords). Fishing rights are disputed; passage rights are enforced by whoever has more ships.
payload.terrain: fast-current passage, first-forming ice, longship-width narrows, groaning ice

payload.summary: A Valdrian observation post on the southernmost rock, manned by two soldiers on six-month rotations. They watch for raiders. They go a little mad by month four.
payload.jurisdiction: Contested between the Kingdom of Valdris (Northwatch garrison) and Hrafnland (jarls of the southern fjords). Fishing rights are disputed; passage rights are enforced by whoever has more ships.
payload.terrain: observation post, southernmost rock, two-soldier garrison

payload.summary: The open water between Tsukuyomi's western shores and Verdania's eastern coast. The crossing takes a week in good weather, two in bad. Trade ships carry Verdania's featherwork, river-pearls, and medicinal bark west; Tsukuyomi's lacquerware, silver, and shrine-craft east. Pirates operate from uninhabited volcanic islets along the route, striking at becalmed ships and vanishing into the fog that the strait is named for. On clear nights the moon lays a road of silver on the water so bright you could read by it.
payload.jurisdiction: International waters. No nation claims the strait. Pirates and weather rule here.
payload.terrain: open strait, week-long crossing, volcanic islets, persistent fog, moonlit silver water

payload.summary: A cluster of uninhabited volcanic islets near the strait's midpoint, honeycombed with sea-caves. Pirates anchor in the largest cave, which has a hidden entrance submerged at high tide. The rock is black and sharp. There are bones in the shallows.
payload.jurisdiction: International waters. No nation claims the strait. Pirates and weather rule here.
payload.terrain: volcanic islets, sea-caves, submerged hidden entrance, black sharp rock

payload.summary: A natural harbor at the strait's midpoint where trade ships shelter during storms. There is no settlement, but there are mooring posts, a freshwater spring, and the remains of a stone shrine to a spirit no one remembers. Ships leave offerings anyway.
payload.jurisdiction: International waters. No nation claims the strait. Pirates and weather rule here.
payload.terrain: natural harbor, mooring posts, freshwater spring, ruined stone shrine

payload.summary: A persistent band of thick fog that sits across the strait for reasons no one can explain. It is not natural. Ships that enter it lose sight of everything, including each other. Some come out the other side. Some do not. The fog smells like cedar and salt and something older.
payload.jurisdiction: International waters. No nation claims the strait. Pirates and weather rule here.
payload.terrain: persistent unnatural fog band, cedar-and-salt smell, disorienting visibility loss

_help: Factions, houses, guilds, companies. `pressure` is the field that makes
one generative rather than decorative: something this group wants that is
not going well, and a sense of how close it is to acting.
NOTE: `pressure` on an organization is stored but nothing moves it yet
(Phase 2, W2.2). Threads already carry a live `pressure`.

payload.summary: The ruling shogunate of Tsukuyomi. The Ashikara clan has held the shogunate for four generations. The current shogun is elderly and has not named an heir. The clan's power rests on the shrine network and the loyalty of the samurai clans, both of which are thinner than they used to be.
payload.wants: To maintain the shogunate's authority over the clans without provoking a succession crisis.

payload.summary: The dragon-bonded knightly order of Valdris. Once the kingdom's strongest defenders, now fracturing between reformers who want to find new ways and traditionalists who refuse to change the old oath. No new dragon bond has been made in twenty years. The order's chapter house in Dragonrest is half-empty.
payload.wants: To remain relevant and powerful in a kingdom that is losing faith in the old bond.

payload.summary: The northern state of Sangguo, ruled by Warlord Cao Shen and his court of scholar-strategists. The strongest of the three states militarily, but stretched thin across a large territory. The truce is three years old and the younger officers are restless.
payload.wants: To reunify Sangguo under Jin's banner before the truce becomes permanent.

payload.summary: The southern state of Sangguo, ruled by Warlord Sun Liang. Wealthier than Jin in trade and agriculture, but militarily weaker. Chu's strategy has always been to outlast its rivals economically. The truce has been good for Chu's treasury.
payload.wants: To maintain the truce long enough to make its economic advantage insurmountable.

payload.summary: The western state of Sangguo, ruled by Warlord Zhang He. The smallest and most mountainous of the three, but rich in iron and jade. Wei's position is defensive — its mountains make invasion costly. The warlord is old and his heir is ambitious.
payload.wants: To secure the mountain passes and maintain independence from both Jin and Chu.

payload.summary: The navigators of the Tide Archipelago — messengers, diplomats, historians, and the only people who can cross open water between islands. The guilds hold the song-magic that makes voyaging possible. They are being strained by the rising seas: more islands need help, fewer routes are safe, and the songs are not always enough anymore.
payload.wants: To find new safe routes and new land for the displaced islanders before the situation becomes desperate.

payload.summary: The old djinn-binding families of Al-Khayzar, who carry contracts with djinn that date back centuries. They govern Zaffar through a council and maintain the Pact of the Lamp. The contracts are their power and their burden — the djinn have been counting the interest, and some of the debts are coming due.
payload.wants: To renegotiate the oldest djinn contracts before the debts become unpayable.

payload.summary: A powerful samurai clan holding the northern mountain province of Tsukuyomi. Disciplined, well-run, and increasingly resentful of the shogunate's neglect of the provinces. Daimyo Takeda Renji is building a coalition of like-minded rural clans.
payload.wants: To force the shogunate to reinvest in provincial defenses and the shrine network, and to position the clan for a succession scenario.

payload.summary: The foremost institution of learning in Sangguo, teaching strategy, philosophy, chi cultivation, and history. Its younger officers are the ones speaking openly about ending the truce. The Academy's archives contain records that predate the three-state division — including a secret clause in the original truce that references something beneath the world.
payload.wants: To maintain its independence from the warlord's court and to pursue knowledge regardless of political consequences.

payload.summary: An ad-hoc council of islanders displaced by the rising seas, formed at Lani Atoll as more families arrive. They are not part of the formal governance structure and have no official voice, but they are growing in numbers and frustration. They want representation, resources, and answers.
payload.wants: To secure housing, food, and a future for the hundreds of islanders who have lost their homes to the rising seas.

payload.summary: The network of moon-god shrines and their miko keepers, led from the Grand Shrine in the capital, that maintain the rituals binding the realm's yokai and warding-stones. Shrine keeper Miko Sora and maiden Yuki tend the capital shrines, but quieter keepers shelter hidden spirits — the tame kitsune Katsura and the hiding yuki-onna Yukina — and the network is split between purity hardliners and compassionate keepers who believe some yokai deserve sanctuary. The network wants to preserve the shrine system's influence and keep the old binding-pacts intact before they fray beyond mending.
payload.wants: Preserve the shrine system's authority and keep the ancient yokai-binding pacts from unraveling.

entries.name: The Five Schools of the Way of Tea

payload.summary: The tea ceremony schools that train chajin and host the quiet, off-battlefield diplomacy of the realm, with tea teacher Satsuki and tea-house owner Hanako among their most visible figures. The schools vie to be named the shogunate's official house style, and their tea houses serve as neutral ground where even Ashikara and Takeda emissaries can meet without drawing steel. The schools want to secure court patronage while preserving the tea house as a sanctuary where clan negotiations can happen in peace.
payload.wants: Win the shogunate's official patronage and keep the tea houses a neutral channel for clan diplomacy.

entries.name: The Forge Guild of the Five Fires

payload.summary: The swordsmiths and blacksmiths of the Kaeden Forge Quarter who forge the blades of the samurai class, with blacksmith Kazue among their working smiths. The guild is bound by charter to supply the Ashikara shogunate first, but Takeda samurai demand blades too, and some smiths quietly forge for both sides to survive the clans' rivalry. The guild wants to protect its secret tempering techniques and avoid being conscripted into open war between the clans.
payload.wants: Guard the secret forging techniques and stay free of forced conscription into the clan war.

payload.summary: The merchant guild (akindo) that controls coastal trade through Kawazaki Great Harbor, where respectable merchants like Machi chase shogunate trade charters while smugglers like Goro run Takeda-sympathetic contraband through the same docks. The guild looks the other way on smuggling for its cut, but the split between charter-merchants and smugglers widens as the shogunate tightens its grip on the harbor. The league wants to monopolize the sea-lane trade and keep the harbor free of direct shogunate interference.
payload.wants: Monopolize the coastal sea-lane trade and limit the shogunate's hand in the harbor.

entries.name: The Consortium of the Counting Coin

payload.summary: The merchant guild spanning Rivenspire's counting houses and Crossford's trade roads, controlling river traffic and the crossroad tolls that fund the realm's commerce. Mead-brewer and merchant Becka Honeymead is one of its many trade-house members. River-merchants in Rivenspire want the tolls kept low while guildmasters in Crossford raise them, and the Greyfen thieves' guild skims from nearly every shipment that passes through. The consortium wants a monopoly on Valdris river-trade and the crossroad tolls that come with it.
payload.wants: Secure a monopoly on river-trade and the crossroad tolls, and crush the thieves skimming their cargoes.

entries.name: The Circle of the Veiled Flame

payload.summary: The circle of hedge-mages, healers, and seers rooted in the elven Groveveil Sanctum of Elfshade, counting librarian Elenna Moonwhisper, fortune-teller Roslyn Vale, healer Isolde Ravenwood, and the hermit elder Rowan Silverbranch among its number. Human mages chafe at the elven elders' caution about teaching higher magic, and the Crown fears unregulated sorcery enough that the Dragon Order keeps the circle under watch. The circle wants a royal charter to practice magic freely, without Dragon Order oversight.
payload.wants: Win a royal charter to practice magic free of Dragon Order oversight.

payload.summary: The thieves' guild and smuggling ring operating out of Rivenspire's Greyfen Quays, where mercenary captain Marcus Briarwood rents blades and the bandit lord Garrick the Wolf launches his highway robberies. The dockside syndicate wants quiet, steady profit, but Garrick's bold raids draw the Harbor Watch and the Dragon Order down on every fence and smuggler in the quarter. The syndicate wants to keep the black market flowing without provoking a royal crackdown that would burn the whole operation.
payload.wants: Keep the black market profitable without provoking a royal crackdown.

entries.name: The Council of the High Houses

payload.summary: The council of noble houses that advise the Crown and guard their feudal privileges, with Baroness Gwendolyn Fairhold acting as political mediator and King Aldran Valdris III presiding from Sunhelm Keep. The northern houses back Prince Roderick's militarism while southern baronesses like Gwendolyn push for mediation, and the Dragon Order's swelling influence threatens noble autonomy on every front. The council wants to curb the Dragon Order's power and restore noble prerogative over royal appointments.
payload.wants: Curb the Dragon Order's power and restore noble prerogative over royal appointments.

payload.summary: The kingdom's dominant religious order, centered on the Cathedral of the Dawnfire in Crownhaven, where priest Evangeline Greymantle and the monk-scribe Galen Frosthollow serve its chapters. The church blesses the Dragon Order's knights as divinely chosen, yet a reformist faction of priests asks openly whether dragon-bonding is holy or heretical, splitting every cathedral chapter down the middle. The order wants Crown recognition as the sole legitimate faith and tithes from every holding in the realm.
payload.wants: Be recognized as the sole legitimate faith of Valdris and collect tithes from every holding.

payload.summary: The merchant cartel of the Five Houses that controls the Silk Road trade through Yunmeng, where information-broker Merchant Zhou Ba plays all three warring states against each other and tea-merchant Su Wanqing feeds the Academy intelligence in parallel. The cartel profits only so long as Jin, Chu, and Wei remain divided enough to outbid each other for silk and spice, and a single misread shipment could bring a warlord's army down on the bazaar. The cartel wants to keep the silk and spice roads open and the three states balanced in perpetual rivalry.
payload.wants: Keep the silk roads open and the three states balanced so none can monopolize trade.

payload.summary: The wandering chi-cultivation sect that trains martial monks and chi-healers across the temples of Yunmeng's Hundred Gods quarter, counting the wandering monk Jian Yi, the chi-cultivation nun Ye Qingrong, and the disguised master Niu Caihong among its hidden ranks. The sect teaches non-interference in the three-states war, yet chi-cultivators are being secretly conscripted as living weapons, and the child prodigy Lin Jiaojiao is the prize all three states now hunt. The sect wants to keep chi-cultivation knowledge out of the warlords' armies and protect the ungifted prodigy from being weaponized.
payload.wants: Keep chi-cultivation out of the warlords' hands and protect the child prodigy from weaponization.

entries.name: The Pavilion of the Jade Diagram

payload.summary: The circle of military strategists and scholar-advisors who convene at the Jade Dragon Pavilion in Chudu, including the Wei master strategist Cao Mengshi, the Jin junior advisor Mei Lin, and the Wei defector-in-waiting He Jingtian. The circle's oath is to the realm rather than any lord, yet every strategist secretly serves a state, and defectors like He Jingtian are hunted by the patrons they betrayed. The circle wants to preserve itself as a neutral brain-trust so that strategy, not mere force, decides the war.
payload.wants: Preserve the circle as a neutral brain-trust that steers the war by strategy rather than force.

entries.name: The Circle of the Still Water

payload.summary: The circle of shamans and spirit-pact keepers who mediate between the tribes and the spirit world, centered on the Still Water Lodge at Iara, where elder shaman Nara and the spirit-pact keeper Yara Moonflower train the heir Iuri Moonflower and the apprentice Tari. The elders hoard spirit-pact knowledge while apprentices are pressed into pacts before they are ready, and the old serpent and jaguar pacts are fraying as the forest itself changes. The circle wants to renew the ancient spirit-pacts and raise a worthy heir before the elder shamans die and the knowledge is lost.
payload.wants: Renew the ancient spirit-pacts and train a worthy heir before the elder shamans pass.

entries.name: The Clans of the Deep Canopy

payload.summary: The coalition of deep-forest hunter clans — jaguar-kin and their human allies — who provide meat, pelts, and the forest-patrol for the canopy tribes, with Kaa the Jaguar-kin, Miri Jaguar-Shadow, Roça Silent-Step, and the night-patrol guard Urutu among their number. The older hunters honor the jaguar-spirit pact and take only what the forest offers, while younger hunters over-hunt to feed the canopy market's hunger for pelts and rare parts. The clans want to enforce the old hunting pacts and keep outsider traders out of the deep forest before the jaguar spirits turn vengeful.
payload.wants: Enforce the old hunting pacts and keep outsider traders out of the deep forest.

payload.summary: The consortium of river-traders and canoe pilots who control traffic on the great rivers and the cascade trade-stairs, counting Amara of the Long Boat, the master pilot Corrente Watersong, the salt-trade leader Suri Salt-Scales, and the message-carrier Bahri Swift-Current among its fleet. The consortium wants to open cautious trade with the outsider metal-people of Dr. Voss's expedition for steel tools, but the shamans and temple guardians warn that foreign goods corrupt the spirit-pacts, and the trader Marcela Good-Trade smuggles outsider wares already. The consortium wants a monopoly on river trade and the profit of careful contact with the outside world.
payload.wants: Secure a monopoly on river trade and profit from cautious, controlled contact with outsiders.

entries.name: The Guardians of the Coiled Serpent

payload.summary: The guardian order that protects the ruined Temple of the Coiled Serpent and the spirit-knowledge sealed within it, led from the pyramid's Serpent's Crown by the warning-keeper Zel of the Temple and the chief's guard Sangue Iron-Heart. The guardians are sworn to keep outsiders from the summit, but the river-traders and the academic explorer Dr. Voss press to study the ruins, and a faction believes the serpent spirit must be re-awakened to defend the forest while the rest insist it stay sealed. The order wants to keep the serpent temple sealed and stop outsiders from plundering its spirit-marks.
payload.wants: Keep the serpent temple sealed and prevent outsiders from plundering its spirit-marks.

entries.name: The Council of the Seven Boughs

payload.summary: The inter-tribal high council of chiefs and elders that gathers in the Seven Boughs Hall to settle disputes and ratify spirit-pacts, with Chief Oron of Iara, the elder council member Sol Many-Seasons, and the genealogy keeper Aja Bone-Remember holding its oldest seats. The council's authority runs only as far as the chiefs will obey, and as the river-traders grow rich and the shamans lose their hold on the spirits, the canopy tribes fracture between modernizers and traditionalists. The council wants to hold the tribes together and prevent open war between the canopy, the river-folk, and the temple guardians.
payload.wants: Hold the tribes together and prevent open war between the canopy, river-folk, and temple guardians.

payload.summary: The council of jarls that meets at the Thing-Mound of Eyrby to settle feuds, elect the High Jarl, and vote on the summer raids, where Jarl Sigrid Hallvarsdottir of Skaldvik holds the High Seat against the young Jarl Erik Stone-eye of the southern fjords, with Gerd Hallvarsdottir speaking for the farming thralls. Sigrid preaches caution while Erik gathers raiders hungry for southern plunder, and the council splits cleanly down that fault line. The Thing wants to keep the peace among the jarls and prevent a civil war over the High Seat.
payload.wants: Keep the peace among the jarls and prevent a civil war over the High Seat.

entries.name: The Carvers of the First Runes

payload.summary: The guild of rune-carvers who cut the binding-runes on ships, weapons, and standing stones from their bothies at Rúnarhólm, with Haldur Blackrune and the bone-carver Hjordis Bonebreeze among its masters. The masters guard the true meanings of the First Runes, but younger carvers sell decorative runes to traders along the Amber-Iron Road, diluting the script's power for coin. The guild wants to keep the secret of the First Runes and stop the cheap-rune trade before it unravels the wards that hold the frost-giants at peace.
payload.wants: Keep the secret of the First Runes and halt the cheap-rune trade that weakens the old wards.

payload.summary: The brotherhood of master shipwrights who build the longships at the Drekahöfn shipyards, where Tor Longkeel, Bjorn Keelwright, and Greta Keelson lay the keels of the fleet. The brotherhood is sworn to build only for jarls who honor the old oaths, yet Jarl Erik's raiders offer double pay for war-ships while High Jarl Sigrid wants the fleet for defense, not raids. The brotherhood wants to keep the shipyards independent of any single jarl and preserve the longship-building secrets for the whole folk.
payload.wants: Keep the shipyards independent of any single jarl and preserve the longship-building secrets.

payload.summary: The loose confederation of raiding crews who crew the longships for the summer voyages south, flocking to the raid captain Astrid Blacktide and the navigator Maren Saltgrief at the Raven Quay. The crews flock to Jarl Erik's promise of rich southern raids, but Astrid remembers the voyage that cost half a crew, and to the young raiders the jarls' caution looks like cowardice. The crews want a profitable, low-casualty raiding season with a lawful share of the spoils.
payload.wants: A profitable, low-casualty raiding season with a guaranteed lawful share of the spoils.

payload.summary: The covens of völur seeresses who read the runes and cast the futures from the Bone-Circle at Hvalhöfn, where the elder Volva Helga and the rune-reader Yrsa Fogborn speak for the sight. The völur see a coming doom — a long winter and a war the jarls will not survive — but the jarls distrust prophecy and the young raiders mock the old women, splitting the coven between those who warn openly and those who retreat into silence. The coven wants to make the jarls heed the warning visions and prepare the folk for the long winter before it breaks.
payload.wants: Make the jarls heed the warning visions and prepare the folk for the coming long winter.

payload.summary: The great spice merchant houses that control the saffron, myrrh, and rare-spice trade from the Saffron Palace in Zaffar, where Layla the Spice Queen holds council alongside the political agitator Yasmin al-Barrani, the rare-spice trader Fatima bint Idris, and the binding-family informant Walid al-Tujjar. The houses vie to fix prices and corner the caravan routes, yet Yasmin agitates openly against the binding families' monopoly on djinn-power while respectable houses like Layla's beg her to keep trade and politics apart. The houses want to break the binding families' grip on city governance and put spice-coin on the ruling council.
payload.wants: Break the binding families' grip on governance and win spice-merchant seats on the city council.

entries.name: The Companies of the Thousand Saddles

payload.summary: The caravan companies that run the desert trade routes between the oasis-cities and beyond, mustered at the Caravanserai of a Thousand Saddles under the desert guide Rashid the Sand-walker, the guard captain Karim al-Qafila, and the porter Omar al-Hamil. The companies pride themselves on safe passage, but banditry on the Broken Road is rising and Karim is, unknowingly, a djinn agent, so some masters pay the djinn for protection while others refuse to truck with bound spirits. The companies want to secure the desert routes against bandits and djinn meddling and keep the caravans moving.
payload.wants: Secure the desert routes against bandits and djinn meddling and keep the caravans moving.

entries.name: The Circle of the Broken Road

payload.summary: The circle of scholars, astrologers, and mathematicians who preserve learning at the Archive of the Broken Road in Khalesh, where the mathematician Maha al-Hisab, the true-name astrologer Tara al-Nujum, the information-broker astrologer Imran al-Nujum, and the elder Yusuf al-Hakim — living archive of the Pact — keep the old knowledge. The scholars seek truth, but the binding families and spice houses want them to justify political claims, and those who quietly study the djinn-Pact's loopholes risk the binding families' wrath. The circle wants free inquiry under a neutral patron and access to the sealed Pact archives.
payload.wants: Free inquiry under a neutral patron and access to the sealed Pact archives.

entries.name: The Wardens of the Broken Road

payload.summary: The city guard that keeps order in the oasis-cities, headquartered at the Warden's Keep in Khalesh, where the night watchwoman Kawthar al-Haras walks the streets and Judge Tariq al-Mir adjudicates by the Pact and contract law. The guard is meant to be neutral, yet the binding families and spice houses both bribe its captains, and Kawthar — having uncovered the corruption — is torn between exposing it and keeping her post. The guard wants to establish an independent, unbribable watch with real authority over binding-family disputes, even over djincraft it cannot fully understand.
payload.wants: Establish an independent, unbribable watch with real authority over binding-family disputes.

payload.summary: The cooperative of deep-water fishers who coordinate the fleet, share the catch, and ration the reef through lean seasons, with the deep-water fisher Rangi Deep-Cast, the reef-walker Moana, the net-maker Tui Lash-Maker, and the chief's son Tamatoa among its crews. The cooperative honors the old rule of shared catch, but the growing refugee population strains the ration, and established fishers resent splitting hard-won deep-water hauls with newcomers. The cooperative wants to feed all the atolls without collapsing the reefs and settle how many refugees the fishing grounds can truly bear.
payload.wants: Feed all the atolls without collapsing the reefs and settle how many refugees the grounds can bear.

payload.summary: The council of island chiefs that meets to settle disputes between atolls, allocate fishing grounds, and decide the fate of the drowned-island refugees, led by Chief Lani of Lani Atoll alongside the refugee former chief Ariki Lost-Chief. The council must decide whether to grant the refugees permanent land or send them onward, and Chief Lani's generosity strains her own people's patience while displaced chiefs like Ariki demand a voice the council is reluctant to give. The council wants to keep the peace among the atolls and find a lasting home for the refugees without breaking the host islands.
payload.wants: Keep peace among the atolls and find a lasting home for the refugees without breaking the host islands.

payload.summary: The guild of tattoo-carvers who record lineage, voyages, and rank in the skin of every islander — the living archive of the Archipelago — where master carvers such as Mana the Tattoo-carver inscribe the route-maps that wayfinders carry on their own bodies. The guild guards the sacred patterns, but as refugees arrive carrying their own marking traditions and some carvers tattoo outsiders for coin, the elders fear the patterns' meaning is being diluted and lost. The guild wants to protect the sacred patterns' meaning and decide whether refugees may earn the marks of a new home.
payload.wants: Protect the sacred patterns' meaning and decide whether refugees may earn the marks of a new home.

payload.summary: The guild of pearl divers who descend the deep reefs for the trade-pearls that are the Archipelago's chief wealth, counting Hina Deepwater, the deep-lunged Vili Deep-Lung, the apprentice Tama Pearl-Blood, and the pearl trader Lio Deep-Pearl who sells their harvest abroad. The divers risk the bends and shark-waters for pearls that traders like Lio sell for a profit the divers rarely share, and the deep reefs yield fewer pearls each season. The guild wants a fair share of the pearl trade and protected diving grounds before the deep reefs are exhausted.
payload.wants: Win a fair share of the pearl trade and protect the diving grounds before the deep reefs are exhausted.

payload.summary: Valdris's border military jurisdiction commanding the forward keeps along the Verdmarch. Held by the High Constable, an office that rotates between noble houses every five years. The Constabulary is underfunded, undermanned, and deeply cynical -- three generations of trench warfare without a single meter of gained ground will do that. The sigil is a crowned iron tower split by a downward broadsword. The motto is 'Not One Span Yielded,' and the soldiers add their own line under their breath: 'and not one span taken either.'
payload.wants: To hold the line without another mass casualty season. To get resupplied before winter.

payload.summary: Verdania's border defense -- a guerrilla network of woodland sentries who contest Valdrian expansion along the northern border. They use living thorn barricades, deadfalls, and pit traps instead of stonework. The Briar Wardens are not soldiers; they are hunters, foresters, and shamans who know the canopy the way a sailor knows the sea. They do not fight in the open. They redirect, ambush, and let the jungle do the killing. The Valdrian trenches face an enemy they can rarely see.
payload.wants: To keep the Valdrian line from advancing south. To protect the northern canopy from logging and burning.

payload.summary: The blacksmiths and siege engineers of Valdris who control the kingdom's military supply chain. Every sword, every shield, every nail in every fortification comes through their forges. They hold quiet leverage over the noble houses -- a lord who crosses the Iron-Forged finds his weapons shipments delayed, his horseshoes thin, his armor rivets soft. The guild masters do not play politics openly. They do not need to.
payload.wants: To maintain their monopoly on military supply. To keep the border wars going -- peace would end their contracts.

entries.name: The Vintner Guilds of Stella Maris

payload.summary: The mercantile cartels controlling Verdania's coastal ports, wine cellars, and trade houses. They produce verdemiel -- the first-pressed floral wine that is Verdania's most valuable export. The Vintner Guilds are urbane, perceptive, and richer than most noble houses. They balance decadent trade with ancestral herbal secrets, and they have no love for the Briar Wardens, whose border war disrupts the northern trade routes.
payload.wants: To keep the trade routes open and profitable. To resolve the Verdmarch conflict through negotiation rather than guerrilla warfare.

payload.summary: The central ruling cabal of Tsukuyomi -- lunar priests and courtly nobility operating from the Shogunal Palace in Tsuki-no-Miyako. The Pale Lotus Court controls imperial ceremony, the shrine network's funding, and the appointment of regional daimyo. They are refined, indirect, and lethal. A word dropped at tea can end a career. A silence held at the right moment can end a life. The Court's power is ceremonial on the surface and absolute beneath it.
payload.wants: To maintain the shogunate's facade of unity while the clans maneuver. To control the succession quietly.

payload.summary: A decentralized network of shrine maidens, shinobi, and information brokers who trade in secrets collected during the midnight hour. The Night-Bell Weavers have no central leadership -- each city has a cell, and the cells communicate through coded shrine-bell patterns rung at midnight. They sell intelligence to whoever pays, including the Pale Lotus Court, the daimyo, and foreign buyers. They are trusted by no one and indispensable to everyone.
payload.wants: To maintain their neutrality and their information monopoly. To keep the shrine-bell code unbroken.

payload.summary: The administrative backbone of Sangguo -- the bureaucracy that manages tax registries, civil examinations, and espionage dossiers across all three states. The Jade Brush Ministry is technically neutral in the Jin-Chu-Wei rivalry, serving whichever state holds the current mandate. In practice, the ministry's loyalties are divided along regional lines, and clerks in Jin'an, Chudu, and Weidu serve different masters while wearing the same insignia. A Jade Brush clerk knows where the grain is, where the soldiers are, and where the money went. That knowledge is power.
payload.wants: To maintain bureaucratic continuity regardless of which state dominates. To keep the examination system fair enough to preserve legitimacy.

entries.name: The Hearth-Kings of the Great Fjord

payload.summary: A confederation of clan jarls from the major fjords, bound by oaths of mutual defense and joint maritime expeditions. The Hearth-Kings are not a government -- they are a pact, renewed every year at the Althing. In practice, the pact holds when the raiding is good and frays when the winter is long. The current pact is fraying. Jarl Sigrid of Eyrby and Jarl Erik of the southern fjords are the two strongest voices, and they disagree on everything except that Hrafnland should not have a single king.
payload.wants: To maintain the jarl system against centralization. To coordinate the southern raids without stepping on each other's claims.

payload.summary: Mercenary hosts that hire their shields to southern wars during the winter thaw. The Boneharrow Companies are Hrafnland's most reliable export -- trained, hardened fighters who take contracts in Valdris, Sangguo, and occasionally Al-Khayzar. They are not pirates; they are professionals. They fight for the contract, not the cause, and they honor the terms precisely. A company that breaks a contract is blacklisted across Hrafnland and cannot hire again.
payload.wants: To keep the southern contracts flowing. To maintain their reputation for discipline.

entries.name: The Grand Academy of the Astrolabe

payload.summary: The scholars and sorcerers of Al-Khayzar who study celestial magic, timekeeping, and mechanical clockwork. The Academy of the Astrolabe operates from Khalesh, the City of the Broken Road, where the best sky-observations in Gaia are possible thanks to the thin desert air and the absence of canopy. They maintain the most accurate star charts in the world, and they will tell you that the stars are not where they were a hundred years ago. They do not know why.
payload.wants: To understand why the stars have shifted. To maintain their monopoly on accurate timekeeping.

entries.name: The Guild of the Water Keys

payload.summary: The subterranean syndicate that controls the qanats -- the deep water channels and reservoirs beneath Al-Khayzar's cities. Without the Water Keys, no city in Al-Khayzar has drinking water for more than three days. They are quiet, patient, and absolutely powerful. The Saffron Houses set prices; the Water Keys set survival. A water-keeper who falls from favor finds his qanat blocked by a rockfall that looks natural. It never is.
payload.wants: To maintain their control over the water supply. To keep the qanat maps secret.

payload.summary: The joint Sangguo-Al-Khayzar trade authority that administers the Silk Pass toll stations. The Toll Guild is technically a cooperative venture, but in practice the two sides skim independently and blame each other for the shortfalls. The Guild's clerks are multilingual, corrupt, and efficient in that order. A caravan master who pays the right bribe passes in a day; one who does not may wait a week for 'inspection.'
payload.wants: To increase toll revenue without driving caravans to the sea routes. To keep the bribe system stable.

payload.summary: An order of master wayfinders who have gone beyond navigation into the deeper applications of song-magic. The Deep Water Singers can call whales, read currents across a thousand miles of open ocean, and sing storms calm -- or call them. They are few, old, and increasingly worried. The songs are not working the way they used to. The currents are shifting. The whales are leaving. Something is changing in the deep water, and the singers do not know what.
payload.wants: To understand why the songs are weakening. To find the whales before they are gone.

_help: People. The player's own character is created with the campaign, not
here — these are everyone else.
`appearance` is prose the image pipeline reads. `visual_identity` is the
anchor that keeps portraits consistent across generations: put the
unchanging things there (hair, eyes, a scar), not today's mood.
`gm_notes` is GM-private and never reaches the narrator or any NPC.
Put what they are hiding there, not in `summary`.
`current_state.location` is LIVE: when the player is at that location,
this person is named to the narrator and the planner as being present.
Use a location id from the block above. `home` is the fallback for
where they are when nothing has moved them.

entries.name: The Guide
entries.gm_notes: The Guide is not a god. They are a remnant of whatever built the Old Roads — a part of the world left behind when the rest took shape. They have been in the Heavenly Realm longer than anyone alive in Gaia. They do not know the future. They know the nations in general terms but not current events. They are genuinely kind but not warm — they do their work and do not explain why. They cannot leave the Heavenly Realm.

payload.summary: A figure who tends the Heavenly Realm. They appear old, or seem old — grey-haired, calm, dressed in simple robes that could belong to any nation. They have been here longer than anyone currently alive in Gaia.
payload.appearance: Ageless and calm, dressed in simple undyed robes that could belong to any of the seven nations. They move slowly, as if time is not a concern. Their eyes are dark and patient. They carry nothing.

visual_identity.hair: grey, long, loosely tied
visual_identity.distinctive_features: a faint mark on the left palm, like an old scar in the shape of a road

desires: To help arriving souls choose a nation to begin in, and to do this work well.
fears_or_limits: Cannot leave the Heavenly Realm. Does not know current events in Gaia. Cannot predict what an arriving soul will become.

entries.name: Miko Sora
entries.gm_notes: Sora has been offered a position at the Great Shrine in Tsuki-no-Miyako but has refused it twice. She refuses because she believes the shrine network is weakening and that abandoning a rural shrine to take a prestigious post would make the problem worse. She has not told anyone this is her reasoning — she says she simply likes the mountains.

payload.summary: The shrine keeper of Haru's Shrine Town. A woman in her late twenties who maintains the ward for this stretch of the Cedar Road. She performs the daily rituals precisely, keeps the shrine grounds, and is the closest thing to authority in the village.
payload.appearance: A slight woman in shrine robes — white top, red hakama pants — with her sleeves tied back for work. She moves with the efficiency of someone who does the same things every day. Her hands are rough from shrine maintenance, not soft from prayer.

visual_identity.hair: black, long, tied back with a white ribbon
visual_identity.distinctive_features: a small burn scar on her right wrist from a mishandled ofuda

desires: To keep the shrine network functioning in her region, even as the central authority neglects the rural shrines.
fears_or_limits: Cannot leave the shrine unattended for more than a day without the ward weakening. The nearest backup shrine keeper is a two-day ride away.

entries.name: Sir Aldrich Whitmore
entries.gm_notes: Aldrich's dragon, Verath, is still alive but has not spoken to him in three years. Aldrich does not know why. He maintains the bond's physical benefits but has lost the dragon's counsel, and he hides this because admitting it would confirm the traditionalists' worst fears about the bond failing. He has been quietly seeking anyone who might know why a dragon goes silent.

payload.summary: A dragon-bonded knight of the order, stationed at Dragonrest. Middle-aged, greying, still carries himself like a man who was once the strongest in a room. He is one of the last knights to receive a bond, twenty-two years ago.
payload.appearance: A tall, broad-shouldered man in worn knight's plate, moving with the careful weight of someone who knows his strength. His armor is well-maintained but old. He has the controlled stillness of a fighter who does not need to prove anything.

visual_identity.hair: brown, greying at the temples, cropped short
visual_identity.distinctive_features: faint scale patches on the back of the left hand — a mark of the dragon bond

desires: To understand why the dragons have stopped answering, and to restore the bond before the order tears itself apart.
fears_or_limits: His own dragon has gone silent. He does not know if the bond is failing or if Verath is hiding something. Admitting the silence would weaken his position in the order's debate.

entries.name: Warlord Cao Shen
entries.gm_notes: Cao Shen is not as healthy as he appears. He has been taking chi-enhancing elixirs that are quietly damaging his heart. His court physician knows but has been silenced. Cao Shen's strategic brilliance is genuine, but his timeline is shorter than anyone realizes. He wants to reunify Sangguo before he dies, and he is running out of time.

payload.summary: The warlord of Jin, the strongest state in Sangguo. A man in his fifties who commands rooms by being the quietest person in them. His reputation is built on a career of military victories and strategic masterstrokes. He is patient in public and impatient in private.
payload.appearance: A lean man in dark robes, moving with the economy of a martial artist who has nothing to prove. His beard is trimmed short, his hair is bound in a topknot, and he wears a jade seal at his belt. He watches more than he speaks.

visual_identity.hair: black, greying, bound in a topknot
visual_identity.distinctive_features: a thin scar along the jawline from an assassin's blade years ago

desires: To reunify Sangguo under Jin's banner and end the three-state division within his lifetime.
fears_or_limits: His health is failing faster than anyone knows. His best general, Lu Fang, is loyal but ambitious, and Cao Shen is not certain the loyalty outlasts him.

entries.name: Shaman Nara
entries.gm_notes: Nara has been hearing something new from the river spirit — a warning about the rising water that the spirit itself does not fully understand. The river spirit is frightened, and spirits do not frighten easily. Nara has not shared this with the council because she does not know what it means yet, and she fears that sharing partial information will cause panic rather than action.
