She suspects the tattoos are helping hold the sea-routes in existence, and that losing wayfinders and routes may be connected to the rising seas, not just a consequence of them.
payload.stakes: If Mana is right, the wayfinders are not just navigating the sea — they are holding it together, and the loss of routes is accelerating the rising waters. This would mean the Archipelago's crisis is partly self-reinforcing: lose an island, lose a route, lose a wayfinder, lose more sea. If she is wrong, it is a theory that wastes precious time.
next_possible_moves: Mana presents her theory to Elder Wayfinder Pua, who takes it seriously — because Pua has suspected something similar for forty years and has never said so.
A wayfinder carrying a faded route-tattoo collapses during a voyage, screaming about pain in the tattoo — the first time the effect has been visible to witnesses, not just felt by the carrier.
Mana begins carving a new set of route-tattoos on Kai, including a route that was lost last month — to test whether carrying a lost route on a living wayfinder can restore it.

payload.summary: The Kaeden Forge Quarter, long the sword-smithing heart of the Tsukuyomi Shogunate, has seen three master forges go cold in a single month. Kazue, a blacksmith who supplies the Takeda clan, claims the charcoal shipments from the eastern hills have been deliberately adulterated with greenwood. Onna-bugeisha Takeda Honoka has quietly opened an inquiry, fearing the sabotage is aimed at weakening the clan's ability to arm its retainers before the next provincial muster. Suspicion has fallen on a wandering charcoal-burner named Goki, a reformed oni trying to live quietly among humans.
payload.stakes: If the forges stay cold, the Takeda clan must buy blades from rival smiths in Tsuki-no-Miyako at ruinous prices, gutting Kaeden's economy and leaving Honoka's regiment under-armed. If the saboteur is exposed, the player could earn the clan's patronage—or make a dangerous enemy of whoever ordered the adulteration.

payload.summary: For a generation the Shirogane Monastery and the Tengu Training Grounds above Yamadera have observed an uneasy accord: humans stay below the treeline, tengu stay above it. That truce fractured when a young monk-in-training was found unconscious at the edge of the Tengu Grounds with his head shaved clean and three black feathers on his chest. Monk Jinichi, sent from the monastery to investigate, believes it is a warning rather than an attack. Wandering tengu exile Suzume fears harder-line elders in the mountain flock are using the incident to justify a full break with the monastery.
payload.stakes: A broken truce means the pilgrimage road through Yamadera becomes unsafe, cutting the monastery off from its lay supporters and stranding the seasonal pilgrims in the Pilgrim Quarter. The player could mediate a renewed accord—or be the spark that turns a cold rivalry into bloodshed on the mountain.

entries.name: The Scouts Who Did Not Return

payload.summary: Three scouts sent from the Kitagoe Scout Hall to map the northern passes beyond the keep have vanished within a season of each other, each disappearing within sight of the border shrine. The last to go missing was a veteran who carved a single warning mark into the gate-shrine's torii before she was lost. Guard captain Daichi, dispatched from the shogunal palace to assess, suspects desertion; the shrine's keeper, Miko Sora, insists the mark is an old ward-sign meaning 'something old has woken.' Meanwhile the Kitagoe Forge has begun refusing to shoe horses headed north.
payload.stakes: If the scouts were taken by something in the passes, the Shogunate's entire northern frontier is effectively blind—bandits, exiles, or worse can move unchecked. Finding the truth could recover lost scouts alive, or reveal that the frontier itself is no longer safe to hold.

payload.summary: A new syndicate has begun levying an unspoken 'toll' on every barge that moors at the Greyfen Quays in Rivenspire, collected by armed men who claim no banner. Harbor Watch captain Brainard Stonewell knows his watchmen are outmatched and has twice been warned off by the Counting Coin guildhall, which quietly profits from the arrangement. Barony mediator Gwendolyn Fairhold has arrived from Crownhaven to broker a settlement, but the smugglers have made it clear that any deal which names them is a deal that ends in fire. The Riven Bridge, the only stone crossing for a day's ride, is the chokepoint where the toll is enforced.
payload.stakes: If the toll stands, Rivenspire's river trade—the lifeblood of western Valdris—funnels silver to an unknown patron, possibly a rival baron. If the watch moves openly, the quays may burn and Gwendolyn's mediation collapses. The player could break the syndicate, take its place, or expose whoever is funding it.

payload.summary: In the Frozen Yard behind Frosthelm Keep, three new graves have failed to freeze over properly—instead the earth above them stays warm and damp even in the depth of the northern winter. Gravedigger Maddox Cinderfell, who dug them, swears the bodies were pallid and unmarked by any wound when he laid them down. The Chapter House of the Pale Vow has sent Scribe Galen Frosthollow to copy whatever records the dead left behind, and he has found that all three had visited the Frost Market on the same day. Healer Isolde Ravenwood, called to examine the exhumed remains, found something coiled in the soil around them that was not any root she knew.
payload.stakes: If the warmth is a sign of something gestating, Northwatch may be one thaw away from a problem none of its defenders are trained for. Solving the mystery could earn the gratitude of the Pale Vow chapter—or uncover a contagion that forces the quarantine of the entire fortress town.

payload.summary: The Silverward Barracks in Elfshade have received no new orders from Crownhaven in eleven weeks. Pay has arrived, but sealed dispatches that should accompany it have not. The barracks' senior elven commander has begun drilling the company in formations that look less like garrison duty and more like a forced march. Retired knight Aldric Stonehand, visiting his old comrades at the Thornwhisper Court, recognized the formations and quietly warned elven elder Lindrel of the Greenhall. The Groveveil Sanctum's wardens have begun watching the barracks in return, and the Moonmarket merchants are quietly moving their caravans out of the city.
payload.stakes: If the Silverward marches without clear orders, it could mean a coup against the Thornwhisper Court, a desertion into the deep forest, or a march on Crownhaven itself. The player could deliver the missing orders, expose whoever intercepted them, or choose which faction to arm.

payload.summary: For nine nights, the oracle-lamps in the Temple of the Lotus Ancestors in Chudu have refused to light, and the ancestral tablets housed there have begun to sweat a thin, scentless water. Monk Jian Yi, passing through on a pilgrimage, reports that the temple's resident priests claim it is merely the season's humidity—but the sweat has appeared only on the tablets of the past three dynasties, all of them houses that fell to war. Jade carver Guo Mingyue, who tends the temple's ritual vessels, has noticed the carved lotus on the great altar has begun to close its petals despite no change in the offering rites. The Floating Lantern Tea House across the canal has stopped hosting the nightly ancestral chants, citing 'a heaviness in the air.'
payload.stakes: If the omen is genuine, Sangguo may be standing at the threshold of a dynastic collapse that the temple has foreseen but not yet named. If it is a fabricated portent, someone is using the ancestors' silence to destabilize the Chu-Jin truce from within. The player could restore the rite, read the true meaning, or be paid handsomely to suppress it.

entries.name: The Granaries That Do Not Empty

payload.summary: The Imperial Granaries of Sanyuan, audited twice this season, show the same grain totals as a year ago despite three provinces drawing from them during a poor harvest. Court treasury official Shen Wuguang, sent from the Chu court to investigate, suspects the books are honest and the grain is genuinely replenishing itself—but he cannot explain how. Magistrate's runner Ai Gulan, the coerced Jin spy embedded in the Yamen, has been ordered to steal the audit ledgers before Shen completes his report. The Ferryman's Quartier is openly whispering that the watermills upstream have been grinding grain that was never planted.
payload.stakes: If the self-replenishing grain is a chi-working or a relic's doing, whoever controls it controls the food supply of three provinces. If the spy succeeds, Jin gains leverage to break the truce on its own terms. The player could expose the magic, steal it for a patron, or keep it secret to preserve the fragile peace.

payload.summary: The Forge Quarter of Weidu has begun producing blades of an unfamiliar dark metal that holds an edge longer than any steel the Stone Sentinel Barracks has tested. Iron mine foreman Tian Baoshan, who secretly deals in qilin-iron, is the source—but he has tripled his price without explanation and refuses to name the new buyer who is outbidding the garrison. Army blacksmith Zhao Tiegun, himself a covert qilin-iron weapons dealer for the Chu state, has arrived in Weidu to find out who is cornering the supply. The Forge Quarter's master smiths are afraid to refuse either of them.
payload.stakes: Whoever secures the qilin-iron supply gains a material edge that could decide the next border clash between the warring states. The player could trace the mystery buyer, corner the trade for a patron state, or destroy the supply to deny it to everyone.

entries.name: The Spirit Nest Has Gone Quiet

payload.summary: The Spirit Nest, the heart of Alta Canopy where the canopy-dwellers go to receive their spirit-pacts, has been silent for a full cycle of the moon. Elder shaman Yara Moonflower, who tends the Nest, reports that the guiding spirits have not answered a single summons—not even the minor ones that answer children. The Seven Boughs Hall has convened an emergency council, but the Hanging Gate, the rope-bridge entrance to the canopy city, has begun swaying even on windless days, as if something is testing it from below. Young spirit-host Folha Green-Laughs has begun speaking in a voice that is not his own during his sleep.
payload.stakes: If the spirit-pacts are truly broken, every ceremonial artisan, hunter, and healer in Alta Canopy loses the source of their craft—and the canopy city's defenses with it. The player could descend to find what has silenced the spirits, broker a new pact, or decide whether the child Folha is a symptom or a door.

payload.summary: The Bone Gate at the Temple of the Coiled Serpent, long cold and sealed by the temple guardians, has begun radiating a low warmth that melts the morning frost off its carved skulls before the sun reaches them. Temple guardian Zel of the Temple, who has spent years warning outsiders away from the ruins, has gone from guarding the gate to refusing to go near it. Spirit-talker Conda Serpent-Eyes, who maintains the old serpent-pact, reports that the pact's binding-songs now produce an answer that comes from beneath the pyramid, not from the sky. The Reclaimed Plaza market has begun attracting outlanders asking pointed questions about the Serpent's Crown summit.
payload.stakes: If something beneath the pyramid is waking, the serpent-pact that has kept the ruins dormant for generations may be unraveling—and the outlanders asking questions may know more than the guardians do. The player could descend into the Hall of Marks, renew the pact, or sell what they learn to the highest bidder.

payload.summary: Three boatloads of salt cured at the Salt Market of Tidal Reach have sickened inland trading partners, and the Saltwater Shrine's water-readers claim the brine itself has turned 'bitter' in the deep anchorage. Salt maker Suri Salt-Scales, who leads the trade journeys, stands to lose the season's entire profit and possibly the consortium's inland contracts. Fisher Toba Net-Caster insists the fish are still wholesome and that the bitterness is being added after the catch, not in the water. The Tide-Moot Hall has summoned both to answer, and the Anchorage fisher fleet is refusing to sail until the matter is settled.
payload.stakes: If the salt is genuinely tainted, Tidal Reach loses its most important inland trade relationship and the river-consortium may collapse. If it is sabotage, the saboteur is still at large in the fleet. The player could clear Suri's name, find the poisoner, or profit from the disruption either way.

entries.name: The Longkeel That Should Not Float

payload.summary: The Longkeel Shipyard in Drekahöfn is weeks from launching the largest warship built in a generation, a vessel commissioned by Jarl Sigrid of Skaldvik herself. Master shipwright Bjorn Keelwright, who oversaw the build, has privately confessed to rune carver Haldur Blackrune that the ship floats 'too high' in the water—its draft is wrong for its size, and no amount of ballast seems to correct it. The Dragon-Prow Works has begun carving a prow-figure that several old hands refuse to touch. Hvalhöfn's flensing crews, in town for the launch, have started laying bets on whether the ship will reach open water or roll at the quay.
payload.stakes: If the ship launches flawed, it could founder on its first voyage—taking Jarl Sigrid's prestige and a fortune in timber with it. If something unnatural is keeping it afloat, the shipyard has built something no one fully understands. The player could uncover the cause, sabotage the launch, or ensure the ship sails regardless.

entries.name: The Ring of the First Runes Is Singing

payload.summary: The Ring of the First Runes, the oldest carved stones in Rúnarhólm, has begun to emit a low humming tone on windless nights that the carvers' bothies can hear through their walls. Volva Yrsa Fogborn, who came north to read the omen, has spent three nights at the ring and returned unable to speak above a whisper, writing that the runes are 'arguing with each other.' Rune carver Haldur Blackrune, summoned from Drekahöfn, has confirmed that two of the stones have altered their carvings overnight—marks no living hand cut. The Fog-Mother's Hut, the seat of the local volva, has begun attracting pilgrims from Eyrby who claim the humming cured an old injury.
payload.stakes: If the runes are genuinely re-writing themselves, the entire foundation of Hrafnland's rune-craft—and the binding-magic that protects its coast—may be in flux. The player could decipher the argument between the stones, harness the changing runes, or decide whether the 'cures' are a blessing or a lure.

payload.summary: The Goldmalt Meadery in Eyrby, the finest mead-house in the southern fjords, owes a debt to a southern trader that it cannot pay in silver—only in a cask of mead aged since Jarl Sigrid's grandmother's time, a cask the meadery swore never to sell. Jarl Sigrid Hallvarsdottir, who counts the meadery as part of her holdings, has forbidden the sale and offered to cover the debt from her own strongbox, but the trader has refused, insisting on the cask or nothing. The Thing-Mound of Eyrby is set to hear the dispute at the next assembly, and the Winter-Eye Granary has quietly stopped advancing grain to the meadery until the matter is settled, threatening the winter brew.
payload.stakes: If the cask is sold, a generational treasure leaves Eyrby and the meadery's reputation suffers a wound it may not heal. If the debt is forced, the trader may call in allied debts across the fjords and trigger a wider trade feud. The player could settle the debt another way, steal the cask, or take the trader's side for a cut.

entries.name: The Archive of the Broken Road

payload.summary: The Archive of the Broken Road in Khalesh, a repository of pre-Pact maps and binding-contracts thought lost, has been quietly re-catalogued by a single unnamed scholar for the past season. The Warden's Keep, which nominally protects the archive, did not authorize the work and only learned of it when a clerk noticed the archive's seal had been re-applied in wax that did not match the keep's own. Elder Yusuf al-Hakim, the living archive of the Pact, has confirmed that at least one scroll removed from the shelves concerns a binding-contract older than the Pact itself—one that names a djinn no living family claims to bind. The Relic Bazaar has begun selling fragments of copied maps that match the archive's distinctive notation.
payload.stakes: If the pre-Pact contract is genuine and unbroken, a djinn of unknown power and allegiance may still be bound somewhere in the desert, waiting for the contract's holder to call it. The player could recover the scroll, identify the scholar, or sell the knowledge to a binding family desperate for new leverage.

payload.summary: A section of the Deep Veins, the gem-mines beneath Naqd, collapsed three weeks ago and sealed off the richest working in the mountain. The Lapidaries' Quarter, which depends on the vein's output, is within days of defaulting on contracts to the Grand Bazaar of Zaffar. The Stone Seat, Naqd's ruling council, claims the collapse was an act of earth and owed to no one—but water-finder Amira al-Ma'in, brought in to assess the stability, found tool-marks on the supporting pillars that were not made by any miner she recognized. Shrine of the Mountain Heart keepers report that the mountain's 'heartstone' has grown warm to the touch for the first time in living memory.
payload.stakes: If the collapse was sabotage, whoever sealed the vein now controls Naqd's gem supply and can name any price. If the mountain itself is unstable, the entire town may be one tremor from being lost. The player could reopen the vein, find the saboteur, or evacuate the town before the next shift.

entries.name: The Well of Mirrors Is Showing Strangers

payload.summary: The Well of Mirrors in Qadira, a scrying-well traditionally used by the oasis-keepers to read the water-table, has begun showing the faces of people who are not in Qadira—some of them dead, some of them never seen before. Oasis keeper Layla al-Waha, who tends the well, has covered it with a pall and refused to let anyone drink, claiming the water 'remembers faces that have not yet arrived.' Water finder Amira al-Ma'in, who dowses for the Garden Quarter's irrigation, has found that the well's water now reads as if it comes from two sources at once. The Dune Rest Caravanserai has reported an unusual number of travelers arriving who match the faces the well has shown.
payload.stakes: If the well is genuinely showing the future, Qadira is about to receive visitors whose arrival has already been written—and someone may be using the well to summon them. If the water is corrupted, the oasis's entire water supply is in question. The player could read the well, identify the strangers, or seal it before more arrive.

entries.name: The Wayfinder Who Forgot the Stars

payload.summary: Veteran wayfinder Hoku Star-Path, who has navigated the open sea for forty years, has begun forgetting the star-paths he carved into his own navigation sticks—paths he taught to every apprentice in the Wayfinder Guilds. He collapsed at the Lani Atoll's chief's float during a welcoming chant and could not complete the route-song for his own home island. Elder Wayfinder Pua, the song-keeper, reports that the chant Hoku was singing when he collapsed was not one anyone recognized, though its rhythm matched the tide-cycle perfectly. Pearl trader Lio Deep-Pearl, who had hired Hoku to guide a deep-water run, is now stranded on the atoll with a cargo that cannot wait.
payload.stakes: If a wayfinder of Hoku's stature can lose the stars, no navigator in the archipelago may be safe—and the canoe routes that connect the islands could unravel within a generation. The player could restore Hoku's memory, learn the unknown chant, or guide Lio's stranded cargo themselves for a share.

payload.summary: The Tide Refugee Council, representing the families displaced from the drowned outer islands, was promised ten new deep-water canoes by Chief Lani of Lani Atoll in exchange for a season's labor rebuilding the atoll's sea-walls. The sea-walls are finished, but only four canoes have been delivered, and canoe builder Solomona Drowned-Home—a refugee himself—has been told the remaining timber was 'reallocated' to the wayfinder guilds' own fleet. Refugee council organizer Vanya Salt-Home has called the allocation a breach of the council's first agreement with the atoll. Chief Lani has invited both sides to settle the matter at the Float Market before the next tide, but tempers among the displaced families are running hot.
payload.stakes: If the council is denied its canoes, the refugees remain dependent on the atoll's charity and the fragile integration of the displaced families collapses. If the wayfinder guilds are forced to give up the timber, their seasonal voyaging may be delayed and the atoll's trade suffers. The player could broker the deal, find the missing timber, or choose a side in the first real rift between the refugees and their hosts.

_help: Prose. Religions, histories, laws, languages, how the world got here.
Do not reach for a record here unless something must point at it, be
counted, appear in a panel, or be hidden from the player. Until then a
paragraph in your world/*.md files is better — see MIGRATING.md.
`context_tier` controls whether the narrator may reason about it:
pinned (always) / partial (one line) / searchable / hidden.

payload.summary: Occasionally a person arrives in Gaia carrying memories of another life — another world entirely. These souls are rare, perhaps one in a generation. They arrive in the Heavenly Realm, where a guide helps them choose a nation to begin in. They are called god-touched, and the name is both a compliment and a warning. They often grow into remarkable people, and just as often into troubled ones.

A vanished network of spirit-paths that once connected every nation in Gaia. Walking a working stretch can take you across the world in an afternoon. Most are broken. Some are lost. A few are deliberately kept shut by the people who live near them. Finding a working entrance is valuable. Using one is noticeable — the Roads leave a trace that certain people can follow.

A generation of relative peace across Gaia, following the last great war between Sangguo's states. The peace is uneven — some nations prosper, others simmer. The treaty that ended the war is fraying, and not everyone remembers why it was signed. The current generation is the first to grow up without war, and some of them do not understand what they would be losing.

entries.name: The Last War and the Treaty of Ash and Salt

payload.summary: Thirty years ago Gaia's last great war ended not with a victory parade but with the Treaty of Ash and Salt, signed in the still-smoldering ruins of a Sangguo border town. The name is literal: each signatory cast a handful of the town's ash and a pinch of salt onto the treaty stone, sealing the oath that no army would cross another nation's recognized border for a generation. The Dragon Order's knights, the Ashikara shogunate's samurai, and the warlords of all three Sangguo states bled in it; the treaty was drafted by exhausted survivors, not conquerors, and no one got what they wanted. Most who fought in it are gone or grey now, and the children raised in its aftermath know the war only as a reason the borders are quiet — which is exactly what the treaty's framers feared would be forgotten.

Gaia's commerce runs on three great arteries and a hundred smaller ones. The Sea-Lane threads the Tide Archipelago to Hrafnland's fjords and Tsukuyomi's harbors, carrying pearls, salt-fish, and amber against iron, furs, and lacquerware. The Silk Road crosses Sangguo's caravanserais and climbs the mountain passes into Valdris, bearing spice and silk toward the northern kingdoms. The Broken Road of Al-Khayzar stitches the desert oasis-cities to the river-stairs of Verdania, where jungle goods meet caravan goods at the cascade markets. Every route pays toll to someone — a jarl, a guild, a binding family, a canopy council — and every route is watched by the people who profit from it and the bandits who'd rather take the cargo than the toll.

In Valdris a dragon's oath once meant something unbreakable — a bond sworn wing to sword, sealed in fire and old language, honored unto death. A generation ago the dragons stopped answering. They did not die and they did not leave; the great wyrms still roost in the high peaks, but they will not speak, will not swear, and will not answer the Dragon Order's binding-calls. The knights say the bond-pact was broken by mortal arrogance; the mages of the Veiled Flame whisper that the dragons saw something on the wind and withdrew. Whatever the cause, the Order still trains its knights in the old rites, performing rituals to an audience that no longer speaks back — and the silence itself has become the kingdom's quietest crisis.

The Tide Archipelago is drowning, slowly, and everyone who lives there knows it. Over the last two generations the high-water mark has crept up the atoll walls until the lowest islands are gone entirely and their people have become refugees crowding onto the higher ones. The wayfinders read the changing currents; the tattoo-carvers now inscribe the maps of islands that no longer exist, so the drowned places are remembered on living skin. No one agrees on why the sea rises — the pearl-divers blame a slumbering sea-spirit, the chiefs call it the world simply changing — but the Council of Atolls must decide how many refugees the surviving islands can hold before the hosts drown alongside their guests.

entries.name: The Truce of the Three States

payload.summary: Sangguo is one nation in name and three in fact: Jin in the north, Chu in the south, and Wei wedged between them, each ruled by its own warlord and each claiming the mantle of the old empire. The Last War exhausted all three without settling anything, and the Treaty of Ash and Salt froze their borders in place rather than ending their ambitions. Open battle is rare now, but the rivalry has simply moved indoors — into the Pavilion of the Jade Diagram where strategists scheme, the silk-road bazaars where merchant houses outbid each other, and the tea houses where poison is quieter than a sword. The truce holds because none of the three can afford to break it, not because any of them has stopped wanting to.

Every nation eats what its land will give and what its trade-routes will carry. Tsukuyomi builds meals around rice, river-fish, and pickled vegetables, with the tea ceremony elevated to a form of diplomacy in itself. Valdris runs on rye bread, root vegetables, river-trout, and mead brewed from the highland hives, with a roast reserved for feast-days. Sangguo layers noodles, dumplings, and slow-simmered broths with the silk-road's spices, and its tea houses serve food as deliberately as they serve tea. Verdania's canopy tribes cook over raised hearths — river-fish, jungle fruit, roasted roots, and game taken under the jaguar-pact — and share every meal as a small ceremony of the tribe. Hrafnland lives on smoked fish, preserved meats, flatbread, and fermented dairy through the long winter, with a great feast meaning someone brought back a whale. Al-Khayzar feasts on dates, lamb, flatbreads baked in clay ovens, and the saffron-and-myrrh spiced dishes that the spice houses trade the world for. The Tide Archipelago eats what the reef surrenders — fish, shellfish, taro, breadfruit, coconut — and a feast is an atoll sharing one catch beneath the stars.

entries.name: The Music and Arts of the Seven Nations

payload.summary: Gaia's nations remember themselves in sound and image. Tsukuyomi plays the koto and shamisen in tea houses and shrine courtyards, paints ink scrolls and lacquerware, and tells its history through bunraku puppet-plays as often as through books. Valdris fills its cathedrals with the Dawnfire choir and its halls with the harp and fiddle of the old bards, while the elves of Elfshade keep a quieter art — illuminated manuscripts and moonlit statuary in grove-stone. Sangguo prizes the guqin and erhu, the ink-wash landscape, and the strategists' habit of teaching history as a verse a child can memorize. Verdania carves its stories into totem-poles and the tattooed skin of its people, and its music is the drum and the bone-flute calling the canopy together. Hrafnland's skalds chant the sagas to the lyre beside the longhouse fire, and the rune-carvers cut the same stories into standing stone. Al-Khayzar fills the night bazaar with the oud and the frame-drum, decorates its mosques and palaces in geometric tile and arabesque, and recites its genealogies as poetry that binding families can recite back ten generations. The Tide Archipelago makes music of the conch-shell horn and the slit-drum, dances its histories in the haka, and weaves its stories into the mat-patterns no atoll weaves quite the same way.

Every nation marks the turning year with at least one great festival, and a traveler moving across Gaia could find a celebration in nearly every month. The festivals are how the nations remember who they are: Tsukuyomi's moon-viewing and blossom-viewing, Valdris's Dragonfire Vow and Harvestmoon mead-feast, Sangguo's Lantern Night and the Three-States Tea Conclave, Verdania's Jaguar Moon and the Serpent-Waking, Hrafnland's Midwinter Blot and Longship Launch, Al-Khayzar's Saffron Harvest and the Night of True Names, and the Tide Archipelago's Pearl Dive and the Rising Tide memorial. Some are joyous, some are solemn, and more than a few are the only day of the year that rival factions will share a table without reaching for a blade.

Across Gaia the unseen world is populated, and every nation sorts its spirits into a different order. Tsukuyomi classifies its yokai from the low mischievous tsukumogami up through the kitsune and yuki-onna to the great kami bound at the Grand Shrine, each governed by shrine-pacts of varying strictness. Valdris names dragons the highest of spirits and treats the lesser sylphs and undines of the mages' circle as minor things, though the elves of Elfshade would argue the old forest-spirits outrank even wyrms. Al-Khayzar binds djinn by true-name under the Pact, ranking them from the lesser ifrit-servants to the marid lords a binding family may call only once in a lifetime. Verdania speaks of a single Great Serpent at the peak of the hierarchy with the jaguar-spirit and river-spirits beneath it, all bound by pacts the shamans renew each generation. Hrafnland counts the frost-giants and the völur's wights as a folk apart from the living, neither worshipped nor bargained with but respected and warded against. The Tide Archipelago reveres the sea-spirits and the ancestor-ghosts of drowned atolls as one tangled hierarchy no carver has fully mapped. The one thing every nation agrees on: a spirit is not a god, and a pact is not a prayer — it is a contract, and contracts can be broken.

entries.name: The Keepers of the Old Roads

payload.summary: The Old Roads are mostly broken, but the few working entrances that remain are not unattended. Each is watched over by a keeper — sometimes a hereditary family, sometimes a lone hermit, sometimes a small order — who lives near the sealed way and ensures it stays sealed, or opens only on their terms. The keepers do not advertise; most Gaian villagers live within a day's walk of a keeper's cottage and never learn what it guards. The shrine network tends the Tsukuyomi entrances, the Dragon Order unofficially watches the Valdris ones, and in Verdania the temple guardians of the Coiled Serpent hold a sealed Road-gate beneath the pyramid. The keepers share one quiet understanding: a working Old Road is more dangerous than a war, because the people who walk it arrive where no one is watching for them.

_help: Objects worth naming. `appearance` feeds the image pipeline; keep story
and provenance in `description`, which the pipeline never reads.

payload.appearance: Small metal discs, about the width of a thumbnail, stamped with the mark of the minting nation. Each is slightly different — Tsukuyomi's carry a crescent moon, Valdris's a crown, Sangguo's a jade-inset square. They are traded by weight, not by origin.
payload.description: The closest thing Gaia has to a universal currency. Accepted across all seven nations by weight. Each nation mints its own, but the metal content is standardized by an old trade agreement that most nations still honor.

payload.appearance: A strip of paper, about the length of a hand, with brush-written characters in black ink. Some carry a red stamp at the bottom. They are usually folded and carried in pockets or pinned to doorframes.
payload.description: The basic tool of shrine magic in Tsukuyomi. An ofuda carries a ward, a blessing, or a command. It must be written correctly and activated by a shrine keeper's ritual. A poorly made ofuda is just paper.

payload.appearance: A carved wooden staff, about shoulder-height, marked with notches and painted symbols that represent star paths, current patterns, and island positions. The wood is dark from salt and handling. Some staves have shells or bone inlays.
payload.description: The primary tool of a wayfinder in the Tide Archipelago. The staff is both a record of routes memorized and an instrument for reading the sea. A wayfinder who loses their staff loses years of encoded knowledge.

payload.appearance: A katana of pale steel with a hamon temper-line that flickers like sheet lightning when the blade catches light. The tsuka grip is wrapped in dark blue silk over ray-skin, and the tsuba guard is iron worked into a swirling cloud motif. The saya scabbard is lacquered black with a single silver crescent at the throat.
payload.description: A legendary blade forged three centuries ago at the request of a shrine keeper who could no longer hold the wild yokai at bay. Raikiri carries a permanent ward along its edge -- a single cut can part a spirit from its manifestation, forcing it back into the unseen. It does not kill yokai; it severs their hold on the visible world, which most yokai find more offensive. The blade has passed through four clans and is currently unaccounted for, last seen in the hands of a ronin heading toward the Cedar Road. Every clan wants it. Most yokai want it destroyed.

payload.appearance: A narrow scroll of rice paper, narrower than a finger, wound around a spool of pale fox-bone. The writing on it is not ink but fine red fox-fur pressed into the fiber of the paper. When carried, the scroll is warm to the touch, like a small living thing held against the chest.
payload.description: The standard instrument of the fox spirit message shops that operate in every Tsukuyomi town of any size. A kitsune writes the message by pressing the recipient's true name and the sender's words into the paper with its own fur. The scroll unrolls itself only in the hands of the intended reader, burns to nothing once read, and cannot be intercepted by anyone who is not the recipient -- the paper turns to ash at a stranger's touch. The fox spirits charge in trade marks or favors, and a favor owed to a kitsune is a debt that accumulates interest in ways no human accountant can predict.

payload.appearance: A bronze bell the size of a closed fist, hung from a cord of braided red and white cotton. The metal is dark with age and etched with a ring of tiny shrine characters that no living kannushi can fully read. It rings with a clear, thin note that carries further than it should.
payload.description: A ritual bell carried by senior shrine keepers on the night rounds of the ward network. When rung with the proper intent, the bell's note silences yokai within earshot -- not by banishing them, but by quieting the part of them that speaks, howls, and draws attention. A silenced yokai cannot call for others, cannot lay a curse, and cannot be heard by the spirits it serves. The bells are consecrated at the head shrine in Tsuki-no-Miyako and only loaned, never given; a keeper who loses one must report to the capital and explain themselves to the head miko. There are perhaps forty in existence.

payload.appearance: A tower shield of layered oak and iron, bound in dragon-scale hide that has darkened to the color of old blood. The iron boss is cast in the shape of a sleeping dragon curled around the grip. The hide still holds warmth even in winter, and faint scale-shadows move across it in firelight.
payload.description: The shield of a dragon-bonded knight of Valdris, fashioned by a dwarven smith and sheathed in the shed scale of the knight's bond-dragon. The bond bleeds into the shield: fire rolls off it, blows that would shatter ordinary oak are absorbed, and a knight fighting behind it fights with a fraction of their dragon's strength. When the bond-dragon dies the shield does not lose its power, but the warmth slowly fades -- a dying dragon's last shed scale is worth a fortune to a traditionalist knight who has not yet received a bond of their own. The order at Dragonrest keeps a vault of shields whose knights and dragons are both long dead. They call it the Wall of Names.

payload.appearance: A lantern of pale silver filigree, taller than a hand and narrower than a fist, hung from a fine chain. There is no candle inside. Instead, a captured point of cold white light floats at its center -- a fragment of starlight gathered by elven sky-watchers on the highest peaks of Valdris on the longest night of the year.
payload.description: An elven-made lantern that burns without fuel and casts a light that reveals what ordinary light hides: hidden doors, concealed passages, the tracks of spirits, and the faint glow of active magic. The starlight inside is a finite thing -- it dims over decades and eventually goes out, and the elven sky-watchers who gather fresh light share it only with those they owe. Valdris elves claim the starlight is not captured but gifted, and that a lantern given in trust burns brighter than one bought. Humans who carry them tend not to argue the point. A lit lantern is worth a year's wages; an extinguished one is worth nothing but its silver.

payload.appearance: A key of black iron the length of a forearm, too heavy to be carried on a ring. The bow is forged into the dwarven rune for 'opening,' and the bit is not a fixed shape but a lattice of interlocking plates that shift and settle against any lock they are pressed into. The metal is cold and slightly oily to the touch.
payload.description: A relic of the dwarven locksmiths' guild of Deep Valdris, forged before the guild sealed its forges. The master-key is not a key to any single lock -- it is a key to the principle of locks. Pressed into a mechanism, its bit rearranges itself to fit, and any mundane lock opens. The key will not open a warded lock (shrine wards, runic seals, djinn-contracted doors), and the dwarven smiths say this was a deliberate choice, not a limitation. There are nine master-keys, each held by a senior guild master, and the guild has not admitted a new master in sixty years. The keys cannot be duplicated; the forging technique died with the last grandmaster.

payload.appearance: A seal of pale green jade, the size of a clenched fist, carved as a coiled qilin with its horn forming the grip. The base is polished flat and inscribed with the seal-script of one of the three states. The stone is cool and faintly luminous in darkness, and the carving is so fine that the qilin's scales seem to shift when viewed from the corner of the eye.
payload.description: The personal seal of a warlord of Sangguo, the physical embodiment of their authority. Every decree, treaty, and commission of state bears its impression in cinnabar ink, and a document without the correct seal is legally nothing. Each of the three states holds one primary seal and several secondary seals for delegated authority. A stolen or forged seal has started at least two wars. The jade itself is said to be cut from a single ancient boulder found at the founding of the first state, and a warlord who holds their seal is believed to carry a measure of the land's chi -- to lose it is a sign that heaven has withdrawn its favor. This is taken very seriously.

payload.appearance: A hand-stitched booklet of bamboo slips threaded on silk cord, the slips darkened with age and the brushwork so small it must be read with a lens. The cover slip bears a single character for 'iron' and the chop of the academy that issued it. The silk cord is frayed and has been re-knotted several times in different hands.
payload.description: A chi cultivation manual from one of the great academies of Sangguo, laying out a specific internal-energy discipline: the Iron Body path, which reinforces flesh and bone against blades and impact. A manual is not a book of spells -- it is a curriculum, a sequence of forms, breath patterns, and meditations to be practiced daily for years. A student who follows it faithfully develops a body that resists steel. The academies guard their manuals fiercely and issue copies only to enrolled disciples who have sworn oaths; a stolen manual is worse than useless, because practicing a form wrong can shatter the body's energy paths permanently. Manuals circulate on the black market anyway, and the academies employ scholars specifically to track them down.

payload.appearance: A flat disc of white jade the width of a coin, pierced with a square hole in the old style and hung on a cord of red silk. One face is carved with the image of a qilin in mid-stride; the other bears a single seal-character meaning 'recognized.' The jade is warm and, in the hands of someone the qilin favors, vibrates almost imperceptibly.
payload.description: A token given by a qilin -- one of the auspicious spirit-beasts of Sangguo -- to a human with whom it has struck a spirit-pact. The token is the pact's physical anchor: while it is carried, the bearer is under the qilin's protection, and any attempt to harm them draws the qilin's attention and, often, its wrath. The token cannot be transferred, stolen, or inherited -- it darkens and goes cold in any hand but its bearer's. When the bearer dies, the token shatters. A qilin gives a token only for reasons of its own, which it does not explain, and a bearer who betrays the pact finds the token does not darken first -- the qilin simply arrives.

payload.appearance: A gourd the size of a child's fist, dried and painted in bands of red, black, and yellow, hung from a cord of woven palm fiber and filled with seeds and small river-pebbles. The gourd is stoppered with wax and wrapped at the neck with a single feather from the shaman's first pact-spirit. Each shaman's rattle sounds different.
payload.description: The primary instrument of a Verdania shaman. The rattle is not a musical instrument but a speaking one -- its rhythm is the language shamans use to address the spirits of river, tree, stone, and beast. A shaman's rattle is built over a lifetime: each spirit they pact with contributes something to it -- a seed, a pebble from their bend of the river, a feather, a shard of bark -- and the rattle's voice grows richer and more specific as the pacts accumulate. A rattle taken from a shaman is silent; it answers only to the hands that earned it. A shaman whose rattle is destroyed must rebuild it spirit by spirit, and some spirits, once silenced, will not speak again.

payload.appearance: A blowpipe of smooth dark hardwood, longer than an arm and bored perfectly straight, wrapped at the grip with cured vine and hung with two or three small clay darts fletched with kapok fiber. The darts' tips are blackened with a paste that has a faintly bitter smell. A carrying quiver of woven reeds holds a dozen more.
payload.description: The hunting weapon of the Verdania canopy-dwellers, used to take game without angering the forest. The darts are tipped with a prepared curare that induces deep, dreamless sleep in humans and beasts alike -- a single dart drops a grown man in a dozen heartbeats, and the sleep lasts hours. The poison is non-lethal at hunting dose, but the same darts can be made lethal with a heavier coat, and the distinction is the hunter's to make. Verdania shamans insist the curare recipe was taught to the first hunters by the river-spirit itself, and that using it on a human without the spirit's leave causes the next batch to fail. Whether this is true or merely prudent folklore is not something the hunters test.

payload.appearance: A smooth river-stone, flat and palm-sized, dark green with a single pale vein running through it like a dried watercourse. When placed in still water the vein darkens and shifts, and faint lines appear on the stone's surface that were not visible dry. The stone is cool and slightly damp to the touch no matter the weather.
payload.description: A divination stone used by the senior shamans of the Verdania river cities. Cast into a bowl of river water, the oracle shows the pattern of the current around it, and a trained reader can interpret the eddies and lines as a reading of what the river knows -- which travelers are upstream, which storms are coming, which spirits are moving. The oracle only answers questions about things the water has touched or will touch, which limits it more than outsiders assume. The most powerful oracles are stones taken from the confluence of three rivers, and the temple-city shamans of the Green Cathedral claim theirs is from the place where every river in Verdania once met. They do not let outsiders see it.

payload.appearance: The carved prow of a longship -- a dragon's head and curling neck in dark oak, the span of a man's outstretched arms, the wood blackened with tar and age. Runes are cut along the neck in a deep, sure hand: wind, wave, ward, and the name of the ship, which is also the name of the dragon it depicts.
payload.description: The figurehead of a Hrafnland longship, carved by a master rune-carver and consecrated at launch. The prow's runes grant the ship beneath them a steady wind on the open sea, a ward against the worst of the waves, and -- if the carving is true -- the attention of no sea-spirit that means the crew harm. A prow is carved for one ship and cannot be moved; when the ship rots or sinks, the prow is cut free and mounted in the jarl's hall as a record of the voyages. A jarl's hall with many prows is a jarl whose people sail far and return. A prow that goes down with its ship is considered still sailing, somewhere under the water, and sailors leave offerings at the shore for the crew.

payload.appearance: A leather pouch containing twenty-odd small bones -- knuckle-bones of seals and deer, a fragment of whale-rib, two human finger-bones yellow with age -- each scratched with a single rune. The pouch is worn soft with handling and tied with a cord of plaited sinew. The bones clatter softly even when the pouch is still.
payload.description: The divining set of a volva, the wise women of Hrafnland who practice the prophecy-visions of seidr. Cast onto a hide in the firelight, the bones' pattern is read alongside the volva's trance-visions: the runes name the forces at work, and the visions show what those forces are doing. A volva's bones are personal and often inherited; the human bones are usually those of a predecessor, kept because a dead volva sees further than a living one. Reading the bones is draining and sometimes shows the seer things she did not ask to see -- a volva who reads too often goes grey early and sleeps badly. Hrafnland respects this and leaves the volur alone, which is the kindest and most practical thing to do.

payload.appearance: A drinking horn the length of a forearm, carved from the tusk of some great northern beast and bound at rim and tip with cold-forged iron. Frost clings to its surface even in a warm hall, and mead poured into it crisps with a skin of ice that does not melt. The iron at the tip is worked with a crude giant-rune no human carver can read.
payload.description: A horn taken -- by trade, by theft, or by finding a giant who had no more use for it -- from the frost giants of the deep Hrafnland mountains. A horn drunk from at a jarl's council grants the drinker a measure of giant-cold: for the rest of the gathering they are unwounded by cold, their words carry a weight that quiets a hall, and their judgement is said to be as slow and final as the ice. The effect fades with the mead. A horn is a serious thing to use -- the giants notice when one is drunk from, and they are patient about collecting favors they feel are owed. Most jars keep their horn for times that truly warrant it, and a hall that drinks from its horn at a trivial matter is a hall whose jarl will not be jarl for long.

payload.appearance: A brass oil lamp, hand-sized, dented and dark with age, the spout curved like a serpent's head and the body etched with old contract-script that glows faintly when the lamp is filled. It holds no wick and no oil -- the interior is dry and smells faintly of smoke and hot sand no matter how it is cleaned.
payload.description: A binding lamp of Al-Khayzar -- the physical vessel of a contract between a binder and a djinn. The lamp itself is ordinary brass; what makes it a contract-lamp is the djinn bound into its terms. When the binder invokes the contract, the djinn manifests and provides the service the contract specifies -- fire, travel, knowledge, protection -- and the lamp records the transaction as a new line of etched script on its body. A family lamp may carry centuries of script, and the oldest lamps are nearly covered, their contracts so layered that no single binder fully understands what is owed. Breaking a lamp does not free the djinn; it triggers the contract's default, which is always worse than the terms. The djinn have been waiting a very long time, and they count.

payload.appearance: A brass astrolabe the width of two palms, its face a nest of nested rings engraved with star-coordinates and the phases of the desert moon. The central alidade is set with a small chip of starlight-glass that catches even faint light. The whole is worn smooth by thumbs and hangs from a cord of braided camel-leather.
payload.description: The instrument of a master caravan navigator of Al-Khayzar, who guides trade caravans across the deep desert where there are no roads and no landmarks but the stars. A skilled navigator with a true astrolabe can fix a position to within a dune-ridge at night and read the stars through the day-star for a rough heading. The starlight-glass at its heart is a fragment of the same captured light the Valdris elves use in their lanterns, traded across the Old Roads in the days when they still ran -- it lets the astrolabe's user take a star-sighting even in the haze of a sandstorm. A navigator's astrolabe is their livelihood and their honor; losing one in the deep desert is a death sentence, and one recovered from the sands is returned to its navigator's family with great ceremony.

payload.appearance: A small quantity of deep crimson stigma-threads, finer than hair, packed in a stoppered glass vial wrapped in oiled cloth. The threads give off a warm, heavy fragrance that lingers in a room for hours after the vial is opened. Even a pinch stains the fingers orange-gold and does not wash off for days.
payload.description: A spice grown only in one irrigated valley near the Mirror Oasis of Al-Khayzar, tended by a single family of gardeners who claim the plants were a gift from a djinn three centuries back and who will not say what they pay the djinn in return. Brewed as a tea and drunk in ritual dose, the spice induces waking visions -- not prophecy, exactly, but a loosening of the boundary between the seen and the unseen, during which a trained reader can perceive spirits, active contracts, and the faint traces the Old Roads leave. Untrained users simply hallucinate, sometimes for days. The spice is sold by the thread at the Star Bazaar at a price that funds the growers' pact for a year per vial, and the demand always exceeds the harvest.

payload.appearance: A disc of polished pearl-shell the width of an outstretched hand, set with thirty-two points marked in tiny drilled holes filled with black pigment and a central pivot of bone. Etched lines radiate from the center in the patterns of the great star-paths. The shell catches light and seems to hold a second sky within it.
payload.description: A navigation instrument of the Tide Archipelago wayfinder guilds, used alongside the wayfinder's staff to fix a canoe's heading by the stars when the horizon is unclear. The compass does not point north -- it points to the star-paths, the rising and setting points of the guide-stars a wayfinder has memorized, and a master can read position, season, and the lean of the current from the way the etched lines catch the night. Each compass is personally calibrated by the wayfinder who carries it and is useless in another's hands, the holes filled to their own star-memory. A compass is given by a teacher to a student upon completion of their long solo voyage and is, after a staff, the wayfinder's most guarded possession.

payload.appearance: A tattooing comb of bone with a row of fine needle-teeth set with black ink-pigment ground from volcanic ash and shark-oil. The handle is lashed with sennit cord and hung with a single small spiral shell that hums faintly when held near open water. The teeth are dark with old ink that never quite cleans away.
payload.description: A tattooing needle of the Tide Archipelago, used by the master tattooers who work alongside the wayfinder guilds to mark a navigator's body with the maps of their voyages. The ink of this needle is mixed under a wayfinder's song, and a tattoo laid with it does more than record -- it marks the bearer's skin with the ocean currents they have crossed, and a navigator so marked can feel the set of a current through the marked lines of their own body, a living compass beneath the skin. A full back-piece takes years and marks a master wayfinder; an unfinished piece marks one still learning. The needles are kept by the tattooers and loaned only to those a guild has approved, and the ink recipe is the most closely held secret of the Archipelago.

payload.appearance: A piece of what was once a path -- a span of paving, a stone threshold, a pair of way-markers -- that clearly does not belong where it is found. The stone is a pale grey found nowhere nearby, and it is warm. Standing on it, the air smells faintly of a place that is not the place around you.
payload.description: A surviving piece of the Old Roads -- the spirit-paths that once connected every nation in Gaia, on which a walker could cross from Tsukuyomi to Al-Khayzar in an afternoon. The Roads are not gates; they are paths, and a fragment is a broken end of one -- a threshold that leads nowhere now, or nowhere a living person can safely follow. Fragments are valuable beyond trade marks because they mark where a Road once ran, and a person who understands the Old Roads (or finds someone who does) can sometimes repair a short stretch. They are also dangerous: the Roads do not check who walks them, and the people who live near the intact fragments often keep them deliberately shut for exactly that reason. A fragment for sale is almost always a fragment someone wants to be rid of.

_help: The opening. One campaign is created from this; you can make more later
in the app.
`player_name` and `character_class` are the player's, and the engine
builds their character record. `current_location` must be one of the
location ids above.
campaign.title: The Arrival
campaign.current_quest: Choose which of the seven nations to begin your new life in.
campaign.opening_scene: You wake in a garden you have never seen. The air is warm and still, and the light comes from no direction you can find. Floating islands drift in soft mist around you, and flowers bloom in colors that do not belong to the same season. Ahead, through a grove of trees that are not quite real, stands an open pavilion. A figure is waiting there, seated on the stone bench, watching you with patient dark eyes. Below the pavilion, far below, through layers of cloud, you can see a world spread out — green and gold and blue and white. Seven nations. The figure speaks: 'You have arrived. That is well. I have been waiting. Come, and choose where you will begin.'
